searchText: parameterisation and risk management of curve's llamma markets methods llamma-based market parameters: a, fee, liquidation discount, loan discount curve’s llamalend v1 markets are permissionless: any actor can deploy a market via the factory without prior approval. this openness makes market creation both accessible and high-stakes, as deployment choices—particularly oracle design and risk parameters—directly influence solvency, liquidation externalities, and borrower outcomes. responsible market deployment, therefore, requires empirical stress testing of collateral assets across representative regimes (e.g., trends, volatility clustering, sharp drawdowns) and systematic evaluation of parameter sensitivity prior to launch. these requirements motivated a design change in llamalend v2, where new market deployments are subject to governance approval, reflecting the need for domain expertise in market configuration. the llamma simulator (“ llammasimulator ”), which was already available with llamalend v1, was developed to support this process by replaying historical price paths, instantiating a llamma-style liquidation amm, and quantifying loss and discount metrics under candidate parameterizations. llamma: liquidation amm mechanism we briefly summarize llamma, the underlying mechanism we are modelling in the simulation. the liquidation amm (llamma) is a continuous liquidation mechanism designed to replace discrete, trigger-based liquidations with a smooth, price-contingent process. it operates over two assets: collateral y (e.g., eth) and debt x (e.g., crvusd), with prices expressed in units of x / y . the mechanism is parameterized around an external oracle price p 0 ​ and a liquidation band defined by lower and upper thresholds p ↓ ​ < p ↑ ​ . band structure and inventory regimes llamma partitions the price space into three regimes: zone y p 0 ​ > p ↑ ​ : the amm cell holds only collateral y . in this regime, liquidation is inactive: the position is sufficiently overcollateralized. zone x&y p ↓ ​ ≤ p 0 ​ ≤ p ↑ ​ : the amm holds a mixture of x and y . trades inside the cell gradually convert collateral into stablecoin as the price deteriorates, implementing partial liquidation . zone x p 0 ​ < p ↓ ​ : the amm holds only stablecoin x , corresponding to full liquidation. this structure ensures that liquidation intensity increases smoothly as the oracle price moves deeper into the band, avoiding sudden jumps in position state. price-dependent amm invariant the core design choice of llamma is to make the amm invariant explicitly dependent on the oracle price p 0 ​ . let x and y denote the current reserves in the band. the invariant takes the schematic form ( x + α ( p 0 ​ )) ( y + β ( p 0 ​ )) = i , where i is constant along a trade, and the shift terms α ( p 0 ​ ) , β ( p 0 ​ ) are monotonic functions of p 0 ​ that govern the transition between pure- x and pure- y states. in curve’s reference construction, the effective internal buy and sell prices of the cell, p ↑ cell ( p 0 ​ ) and p ↓ cell ( p 0 ​ ) , are chosen such that: they coincide with p 0 ​ at the band edges, they move away from p 0 ​ outside the band, and they ensure arbitrage consistency with the external market. a convenient parameterization expresses the band width via a single amplification parameter a , with p ↑ ​ p ↓ ​ ​ = a a − 1 ​ , which controls how aggressively inventory shifts as price moves across the band. economic interpretation llamma can be interpreted as embedding the borrower’s collateral into a price-conditioned amm trajectory . instead of liquidating a position at a single trigger price, collateral is continuously swapped into stablecoin as the oracle price declines. this achieves three objectives simultaneously: smoother liquidation paths, reduced liquidation externalities, and endogenous price impact through the amm itself. crucially, llamma defines liquidation not as a discrete event, but as a state-dependent trading process, fully determined by ( p 0 ​ , a , p ↓ ​ , p ↑ ​ ) . simulation framework the llammasimulator implements a path-replay simulation of the llamma liquidation mechanism under historical price dynamics. given a time series of market prices, the simulator deterministically replays the evolution of a llamma-style banded amm, tracking inventory traversal, fee accumulation, and portfolio value over time. the objective is to quantify pathwise deterioration of a representative llamma position under realistic volatility regimes and to summarize this deterioration using tail-risk statistics suitable for parameter comparison and risk calibration. price input and preprocessing the simulator takes as input a historical ohlcv time series sampled at a fixed resolution (e.g. one-minute candles). each observation is of the form ( t i ​ , o i ​ , h i ​ , l i ​ , c i ​ , v i ​ ) , where t i ​ denotes the timestamp and h i ​ , l i ​ define the intraperiod price range. it is key to have a sufficiently long period of price data; we settle on 4 years’ worth of data on a 1-minute timeframe, as this historically represents a crypto cycle, meaning shows a set of diverse market conditions. note: the data we feed to the simulation should be close to what the market will see on-chain. data availability issues when an asset lacks sufficient historical price data to support direct simulation (typically < 4 years of minute-level ohlcv), we extend the framework using proxy-based path construction with explicit uncertainty accounting. assets are handled under two cases. if partial history is available, we compute scale-free return statistics (annualized volatility, kurtosis, jump frequency, and first-order autocorrelation) on the overlapping window between the new asset and a set of candidate reference assets. these metrics are normalized and compared in feature space, and the reference asset with the minimal distance is selected as the closest proxy. the new asset’s observed price path is retained where available, and its missing pre-history is filled using the proxy asset’s return path aligned to the same sampling frequency. if no usable history exists, the asset is directly assigned to a conservative reference class (e.g., high-volatility governance tokens), and the full simulated path is derived from that reference. in both cases, proxy use introduces model risk. we therefore compute an explicit uncertainty score based on data coverage and proxy dissimilarity, and apply this as a multiplicative buffer to the resulting liquidation and loan discounts. this ensures that parameter recommendations remain conservative under data scarcity and are relaxed only as native price history accumulates. oracle construction llamma liquidation dynamics depend on an oracle price rather than the raw market price. in the simulator, the oracle price p t ​ is constructed as an exponential moving average (ema) of intraperiod mid-prices: m i ​ = 2 1 ​ ( h i ​ + l i ​ ) , p i ​ = α i ​ m i ​ + ( 1 − α i ​ ) p i − 1 ​ , α i ​ = 1 − 2 − δ t i ​ / t e x p ​ , where t e x p ​ is the ema half-life (in seconds) and δ t i ​ is the elapsed time since the previous observation. this oracle smoothing introduces inertia into band boundaries and fee dynamics, reflecting the fact that llamma liquidation thresholds evolve continuously rather than instantaneously with spot prices. effective price bounds and external friction at each timestep, the simulator evaluates whether the llamma position would be arbitraged given the candle’s high–low range. to approximate execution frictions external to llamma (e.g., routing costs, taker fees, residual slippage), the raw bounds are widened via an external fee parameter ϕ : h i eff ​ = h i ​ ( 1 − ϕ ) , l i eff ​ = l i ​ ( 1 + ϕ ) . trades are triggered only if these effective bounds cross the current amm price, ensuring that simulated rebalancing corresponds to economically viable arbitrage opportunities. llamma state initialization each simulation run represents a single hypothetical loan position. at the start of the run, a fixed quantity of collateral (normalized to one unit) is deposited across a discrete set of liquidation bands above the current oracle price. the number of bands (range_size) and their geometric spacing are determined by the amplification parameter (a), consistent with llamma’s band construction. this initial state represents a freshly opened position prior to any adverse price movement. all subsequent changes in portfolio value arise endogenously from price evolution, band traversal, and fees. deterministic band traversal for each candle, the simulator performs the following steps: oracle update: the oracle price p t ​ is updated using the ema rule. target price mapping: the effective high and low prices are mapped into llamma’s internal price space, accounting for band-specific fees and oracle-relative distortions. arbitrage-driven rebalancing: if the effective high exceeds the current amm price, the simulator deterministically trades upward , selling collateral and moving inventory toward higher bands. if the effective low falls below the amm price, it trades downward , buying collateral and moving inventory toward lower bands. cross-band execution: trades proceed band by band. within each band, the llamma invariant is respected exactly; if a band is exhausted, the active band index is updated and trading continues until the target price is reached or no further arbitrage is possible. this procedure produces a fully deterministic inventory path conditional on the price series and parameter set. fee dynamics each trade is subject to an effective fee that combines multiple components: a base fee , representing static protocol costs; an oracle-movement fee , increasing with recent oracle volatility and decaying over time; an optional distance-based fee , increasing with deviation from the oracle price. at each band crossing, the applicable fee is applied asymmetrically depending on trade direction, reducing the effective target price when selling and increasing it when buying. fees are accumulated implicitly through reduced inventory conversion, directly impacting portfolio value. portfolio valuation at any time t , the total portfolio value is expressed in the debt asset x by adiabatically converting all band inventories to x at the prevailing oracle price. this produces a single scalar value v t ( x ) ​ independent of the current band configuration. for a simulation window [ t 0 ​ , t 1 ​ ] , the realized loss is defined ℓ = 1 − v t 0 ​ ( x ) ​ v t 1 ​ ( x ) ​ ​ loss is reported as a unitless relative measure, defined as the fractional change in portfolio value in a fixed numeraire. sampling of loan windows rather than simulating a single contiguous trajectory, the simulator samples many random loan windows from the historical dataset. each window is defined by: a random start position within the dataset; a fixed or bounded duration expressed in days. for each window, the full simulation described above is executed independently, producing one loss observation. this sampling scheme approximates the distribution of outcomes faced by loans initiated at arbitrary points in time. tail-loss aggregation given a collection of loss observations ( ℓ 1 ​ , … , ℓ s ​ ), the simulator focuses on the upper tail of the distribution. losses are sorted in descending order, and the reported statistic is the mean of the worst m observations: es m / s ​ = m 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 m ℓ ( i ) ​ this tail-average loss is an empirical analogue of expected shortfall and is used as the primary objective for parameter comparison. it emphasizes adverse but plausible scenarios, aligning with the risk-management goals of liquidation parameterization. llamma simulator v2 the llammalend v2 simulator preserves the core of the original llamma simulator. the primary changes are architectural refactoring, a revised fee simulation model, and the introduction of explicit stress amplification mechanisms. worst day scaling a key new feature in the v2 simulator is worst-day scaling , an optional stress-testing mode that amplifies adverse price movements within sampled windows. in practice, worst-day scaling is enabled by selecting the v2 mode ( is_v2=true ), which switches the price loader from genericpricehistoryloader (raw replay) to volatilitypricehistoryloader (drawdown-rescaled windows) in the experiment runners (e.g., see calculation.py simulate_fee / simulate_a ). when enabled, the simulator first scans the full ohlcv dataset to identify the maximum intraperiod drawdown—defined as the largest peak-to-trough decline from high h i ​ to low l i ​ ​ over any window of a fixed duration. during simulation, instead of replaying a randomly sampled price window verbatim, the sampled window is rescaled so that its internal drawdown matches the worst observed drawdown. concretely, prices within the window are transformed via an affine scaling around the window’s maximum price, leaving the local structure of returns intact while increasing the amplitude of adverse movements. the resulting path preserves temporal ordering and relative price dynamics but enforces a worst-case drawdown magnitude. worst-day scaling is intended to emulate more severe but historically anchored stress scenarios, particularly for assets whose realized volatility during the evaluation horizon may underrepresent plausible downside risk. it is best interpreted as a conditional stress test rather than a probabilistic forecast. analysts should note that this transformation alters the effective return distribution of the asset: while relative intrawindow dynamics are preserved. it can be useful for assets with shorter price history (i.e., that experience one or two extreme events). market parameterisation experiments using the simulation framework described above, we perform targeted parameter sweeps to identify economically and risk-efficient llamma configurations. configurable parameters the simulator parameters can be grouped into three categories: price data inputs (historical ohlc series and preprocessing choices), contract parameters (e.g., a, fee, oracle settings), behavioural assumptions (e.g., range size, liquidation duration, external friction) simulation controls (e.g., sampling, tail level, seed). we now discuss each category in detail. price data inputs we typically recommend obtaining 4 years' worth of 1-min price data from a trustworthy data source that reasonably represents the collateral debt relationship. for bluechip assets and large-cap, alt-coins, binance is often a good resource. for instance, to parameterize the tbtc-crvusd market, the btc-usdt feed was used. for additional data, one can load the existing inverted by setting add_reverse to false . we generally do not enable this if not needed, to avoid assuming symmetry in price action for up and down movements. data availability issues when an asset has insufficient price history to run the 4-year, 1-minute replay, we treat this as explicit model risk and switch to a proxy-and-buffer procedure. choosing the right asset still requires expert judgement and careful qualitative consideration of assets selected. case 1 — partial history (< 4 years). let the asset have returns r t ( a ) ​ on its available window. we compare it to candidate references j ∈ r on the common overlapping window using a scale-free feature vector f ( x ) = ( σ ann ​ ( x ) , κ ( x ) , π 3 σ ​ ( x ) , ρ 1 ​ ( x ) ) , where σ ann ​ is annualized realized vol, κ kurtosis, π 3 σ ​ jump frequency pr ( ∣ r ∣ > 3 σ ) , and ρ 1 ​ acf(1). after z-scoring features across candidates, we select the closest proxy j ∗ = ar g min j ∈ r ​ ∣ f ~ ( a ) − f ~ ( j ) ∣ 2 ​ . we then construct a synthetic pre-history by splicing the asset’s observed segment with the proxy’s return dynamics for the missing period (returns-based, hence scale-free), yielding an effective 4-year series for the replay. case 2 — no usable history. we cannot compute f ( a ) , so we choose a conservative reference class (e.g., high-vol governance-token basket) and treat uncertainty as maximal by construction. uncertainty buffer (both cases). we assign an uncertainty score u ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] combining (i) similarity error (distance in feature space) and (ii) coverage shortfall (how far we are from 4 years). this score drives conservative parameter uplifts, e.g. l i q _ d i sco u n t f ina l = l i q _ d i sco u n t s im × ( 1 + λ u ) , l o an _ d i sco u n t f ina l = l o an _ d i sco u n t s im × ( 1 + λ u ) , with λ a governance-chosen conservatism factor. as more native history accrues, it decreases mechanically (coverage increases and similarity can be re-estimated), and parameters can be tightened accordingly. contract parameter contract parameters are values defined by deployed contracts (immutable or governance-controlled) that structurally determine llamma and oracle behavior. these parameters include: a : the amplification coefficient or also known as the bandwidth factor) defines the density of the liquidity and band size. it can be looked onchain within the llamma contract (e.g., see sdola-crvusd market llamma contract under the public method ‘a’ ). fee : the base fee charged in llamma to arbitrageurs and paid to the borrower. it can be looked onchain within the llamma contract (e.g., see sdola-crvusd market llamma contract under the public method ‘fees’ ). dynamic_fee_multiplier : is the hard-coded sensitivity of the llamma amm fee to deviations between the oracle price and the in-band price , used to penalize rapid or out-of-band price moves and protect the amm from oracle jumps. it is not configurable at deployment or by governance and fixed in the amm code as a ¼ coefficient and can be found in the llamma contract under get_dynamic_fee() . texp : the exponential moving-average window used by the external price feed consumed by llamma. it should be read from the underlying oracle contract ; if multiple pools are chained, we recommend using the shortest ma window (smallest ma_time / exp_ma_time ) as it governs the fastest price response. the relevant pool address is exposed on-chain via the oracle’s public pool method, and the ma parameter can be read directly from that pool contract (e.g., see sdola-crvusd market oracle contract under the public method ‘pool’ and within the pool contract under exp_ma_time ). behavioural parameters behavioural assumptions are analyst-chosen assumptions about liquidation, arbitrage, and liquidity placement that are not enforced on-chain but materially affect tail losses and stress outcomes. these parameters include: min_loan_days/max_loan_days: bound the assumed liquidation duration in the simulation. each run samples a window within this range (typically between 30 to 60 minutes); longer windows typically increase price exposure and tail losses, shorter windows approximate faster liquidations and reduce losses. range_size : the number of bands used to initialize a position in the simulation. for conservative parameterization, this is set to 4 , as it concentrates liquidity into the fewest allowed bands, reducing price-absorption capacity and causing bands to deplete faster, which maximizes worst-case (liquidation-style) losses. larger ranges spread liquidity more evenly and mechanically lower tail losses. external_fee : the transaction cost paid by arbitrageurs when routing trades outside llamma (e.g., dex fees, aggregator fees, and gas). in the simulation, it is modeled as an exogenous spread that reduces the effective price improvement arbitrageurs can capture, thereby weakening arbitrage pressure and increasing residual inventory loss inside the amm. higher external fees delay rebalancing and raise worst-case losses; setting it to zero assumes frictionless arbitrage and yields a lower-bound loss estimate. simualtion parameters simulation parameters are technical settings that control how losses are estimated (sampling, tails, determinism) without changing the underlying economic mechanism. these parameters include: samples : the number of monte carlo liquidation paths drawn from the historical price series; higher values reduce estimation error, while the deterministic mode evaluates all admissible windows without resampling. n_top_samples : the number of worst-loss realizations averaged to compute expected shortfall, controlling the granularity of tail-risk estimation for a given sample size. tails.liquidation : the tail probability used to estimate the liquidation discount, corresponding to the expected shortfall of the worst α fraction of simulated losses. tails.loan : the tail probability used to estimate the loan discount, targeting a deeper tail than liquidation to provide an additional solvency buffer at loan origination. seed : the random seed used for monte carlo sampling to ensure reproducibility of stochastic experiments. finding the fee parameter the internal fee controls the trade-off between liquidation efficiency and inventory protection . low fees allow inventory to traverse bands with minimal friction but expose the amm to adverse selection during volatile price movements. high fees, conversely, reduce adverse selection but increase cumulative loss by inhibiting timely re-centering. to identify an appropriate fee level, we perform a one-dimensional sweep over candidate fee values while holding all other parameters fixed. for each fee, the simulator estimates the tail-average loss over randomly sampled loan windows. the resulting loss curve is typically convex: losses decrease initially as fees provide protection, then increase once excessive friction dominates. source: llammasimulator v2 - eth/usdt fee experiment the fee is selected at the minimum of this loss curve , corresponding to the point where marginal protection from higher fees is exactly offset by marginal execution inefficiency. this criterion directly aligns the fee choice with observed tail risk rather than average-case performance. finding the amplification parameter (a) the amplification parameter (a) determines the geometric spacing of liquidation bands and thus governs how finely collateral is distributed across price levels. smaller (a) produces coarse bands with abrupt inventory transitions, while larger (a) yields finer ladders at the cost of increased traversal and fee accumulation. given a fixed fee (as determined above), we perform a sweep over (a) and evaluate two complementary quantities: the tail-average loss , capturing realized deterioration under dynamic price paths; and a liquidation discount proxy , which adjusts the loss by the static geometry of the band ladder and reflects the disadvantage of unwinding deeper bands first. source: llammasimulator v2 - eth/usdt a experiment the optimal amplification a ∗ is chosen at the minimum of the liquidation discount curve (orange) , representing the balance between volatility absorption and re-centering cost. the liquidation discount is then read off the loss curve (blue) at this same a ∗ , ensuring that both parameters are internally consistent and jointly calibrated to empirical tail behavior. finding the liquidation discount the liquidation discount is used to discount the collateral for calculating the recoverable value upon liquidation at the current market price. given that we are sampling a random segment of the historical sample data, we are not necessarily covering every scenario of the historical data. sampling is necessary as we are conducting parameter sweeps across parameters, which in turn becomes costly. yet, for a fixed a and fixed fee, key parameters are already determined, meaning sweeps are not necessary anymore. this allows us to switch to deterministic sampling. hence, we recommend that once the fee and a are determined, re-run without sampling and use the resulting loss as the market liquidation discount. generally, we are looking at the top 1% worst losses resulting from the simulation, which, for 4-year 1-min data on a 1h time window, roughly corresponds to 200 cases. finding the loan discount the loan discount is the percentage used to discount the collateral for calculating the maximum borrowable amount when creating a loan. loan discount has been in the v1 version, historically just received a 3 percent margin to the liquidation_discount. we instead recommend defining the loan discount margin endogenously from the simulated loss distribution. specifically, we set the margin based on the gap between two extreme quantiles of deterministic losses: for example, the difference between the 1% tail and the 0.25% tail (approximately the worst 200 versus the worst 50 scenarios). this margin captures the slope of the extreme tail , providing a statistically grounded buffer that accounts for how rapidly losses escalate beyond the liquidation threshold. this construction ensures that newly opened loans remain solvent even if market conditions deteriorate from severe to extreme, while avoiding arbitrary buffers that may be either insufficient or overly restrictive. note: currently we maintain to regardless of identified margin, a minimum margin requirement of 3% for uncorrelated assets and 0.5% fo correlated assets. online monitoring of loan & liquidation discount once a market is deployed, core structural parameters of the llamma mechanism are fixed and cannot or are unlikely to change. in this case, the llammasimulator can be repurposed from a parameter-search tool into a deterministic monitoring framework that continuously re-estimates the implied loan and liquidation discounts under evolving market conditions. objective the objective of online monitoring is to detect whether the risk buffers implied by recent market dynamics remain aligned with the discounts currently enforced on-chain. rather than re-optimizing (a) or fees, the framework recomputes liquidation and loan discounts using the deployed configuration and compares them to the active parameters, providing an evidence-based signal for governance review. a stylised flow is displayed below: ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ scheduler / trigger (weekly)│ └──────────────┬───────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ fetch market configuration │ └──────────────┬───────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ config comparator │ │ (a, fee, texp vs last run) │ └───────┬───────────┬──────────┘ │ │ │ changed │ unchanged ▼ ▼ ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ full simulation│ │ incremental simulation │ │ (expensive) │ │ - run only new days │ │ │ │ - drop oldest days (4y) │ └───────┬────────┘ └──────────────┬───────────────┘ │ │ └──────────────┬───────────┘ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ simulation cache │ │ (rolling 4y window) │ └──────────────┬───────────────┘ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ discount comparator │ │ loan_discount vs current_loan│ │ liq_discount vs current_liq │ └──────────────┬───────────────┘ │ ┌───────────────┴─────────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ governance proposal │ │ no action │ │ adjusting parameters │ └────────────────────────┘ └────────────────────────┘ deterministic simulation update at each monitoring run, the simulator executes a deterministic path-replay over a fixed rolling evaluation horizon using the current market configuration: price data loading. historical ohlc data are loaded with sufficient warmup to ensure oracle convergence. all timestamps and evaluation boundaries are defined centrally to guarantee consistency across runs. rolling window evaluation. losses are computed over a deterministic grid of rolling windows (fixed window length and stride) covering the evaluation horizon. this replaces random sampling and ensures reproducibility. incremental computation. previously computed windows are reused. only new windows since the last run are simulated, while windows falling outside the horizon are discarded. if the market configuration changes, the cache is invalidated, and the horizon is recomputed in full. tail aggregation. window losses are aggregated into tail-average loss statistics, from which implied liquidation and loan discounts are derived using the same mapping as in initial parameterization. decision rule the monitoring output consists of updated estimates of liq_discount and loan_discount . these are compared to the corresponding on-chain parameters: if deviations exceed a predefined tolerance (i.e., currently 1% difference), a governance update is triggered. the system does not perform automatic parameter updates; it provides a structured, reproducible risk signal to support governance decisions. limitation and future research in this section, we discuss the key limitations and areas for future research: unseen tail events: the framework is inherently historical and path-based: it cannot guarantee coverage of extreme regimes that have not occurred in the observed data (e.g., novel market structure failures, sudden delistings, protocol-specific exploits). as a result, estimated tail losses may understate true worst-case risk. a future improvement to the methodology utilises generative pricing models informed by the statistical properties of the time series. this will allow us to amplify specific properties (e.g., jump frequency or volatility) of the series and enable us to test for scenario more extreme than have been observed historically in the data. regime and structural breaks. the methodology assumes stationarity of return dynamics. fundamental shifts in an asset’s behavior—such as changes in utility, liquidity venues, tokenomics, regulatory status, or holder composition—can invalidate historical similarity and cause proxy-based estimates to become unreliable. with the online monitoring framework, we attempt to mitigate this, yet in the future, more sophisticated regime detection may be a promising area of future research. proxy misclassification risk. for assets with partial or no history, risk parameters rely on reference assets selected via statistical similarity. even with conservative buffers, an incorrect proxy choice can lead to systematic mis-estimation of liquidation and loan risk. these limitations imply that results should be interpreted as risk-informed lower bounds under modeled conditions, not as guarantees of solvency. continuous monitoring, periodic re-parameterization, and governance oversight remain necessary as market conditions evolve. conclusion this work formalizes a reproducible, tail-risk–focused methodology for llamma market parameterization, combining path-replay simulation, conservative stress testing, and explicit uncertainty handling. by grounding fee, amplification, and discount choices in empirical worst-case behavior—while retaining governance oversight and continuous monitoring—the framework provides a robust lower-bound assessment of liquidation risk that can be systematically updated as market conditions and data availability evolve.

excerpt: The methodology attempts to estimates a safe upper bound for YieldBasis (YB) exposure relative to the absorption capacity of Curve PegKeeper (PK) pools. The core assumption is that YB unwind activity may generate net crvUSD sell p
searchText: yb safe caps methods the methodology attempts to estimates a safe upper bound for yieldbasis (yb) exposure relative to the absorption capacity of curve pegkeeper (pk) pools. the core assumption is that yb unwind activity may generate net crvusd sell pressure into pegkeeper pools. as pegkeeper pools become increasingly imbalanced toward crvusd, stable-side liquidity becomes depleted, increasing slippage and potentially impairing peg stability. the methodology therefore attempts to estimate how much yb exposure can be supported by the remaining stable-side liquidity available across pegkeeper pools. the original framework used a static heuristic based on aggregate pegkeeper tvl. the safe yb exposure ceiling was defined as: s m a x ​ = m y b ​ ⋅ f safe ​ ⋅ t v l p k ​ where t v l p k ​ is the aggregate pegkeeper pool tvl, f safe ​ is the assumed maximum safe crvusd pool fraction, and m y b ​ is a stress multiplier mapping yb exposure into effective crvusd sell pressure. the methodology used: f safe ​ = 0.75 and: m y b ​ = 2.5 resulting in: s m a x ​ = 2.5 × 0.75 × t v l p k ​ the interpretation of the framework is that pegkeeper pools are assumed capable of safely absorbing crvusd inflows until approximately 75% of pool inventory consists of crvusd. the quantity: f safe ​ ⋅ t v l p k ​ therefore represents the assumed safe amount of crvusd inventory that pegkeeper pools can hold before stable-side liquidity becomes excessively depleted. the multiplier m y b ​ scales this quantity into a maximum yb exposure ceiling under the assumption that yb unwind activity may amplify effective crvusd sell pressure under adverse market conditions. the limitation of the static methodology is that it assumes all pegkeeper tvl contributes equally to absorption capacity regardless of current pool state. consequently, balanced pools and already heavily crvusd-skewed pools receive identical treatment, despite possessing materially different remaining stable-side liquidity. the methodology therefore estimates total theoretical absorption capacity, but not remaining real-time capacity. to address this limitation, the methodology was extended into a state-dependent framework that incorporates the current imbalance state of pegkeeper pools. for each pegkeeper pool, imbalance is computed as: i ( t ) = b crvusd ​ ( t ) + b stable ​ ( t ) b crvusd ​ ( t ) − b stable ​ ( t ) ​ where b crvusd ​ ( t ) is the crvusd balance and b stable ​ ( t ) is the corresponding stablecoin balance. the imbalance is then transformed into the crvusd inventory share: s crvusd ​ ( t ) = 2 1 + i ( t ) ​ such that s crvusd ​ = 0.5 corresponds to a balanced pool, s crvusd ​ > 0.5 corresponds to a crvusd-heavy pool, and s crvusd ​ < 0.5 corresponds to a stable-heavy pool. to reduce sensitivity to transient fluctuations, the imbalance series is exponentially smoothed using an ema: s crvusd em a ​ ( t ) the state-dependent safe exposure ceiling is then defined as: s m a x ​ ( t ) = m y b ​ ⋅ [ f safe ​ max ( 0 , s crvusd em a ​ ( t ) − 0.5 ) ] ⋅ t v l p k ​ ( t ) with: f safe ​ = 0.70 and: m y b ​ = 2.5 under this framework, the full safe fraction f safe ​ is used whenever pegkeeper pools are balanced or stable-heavy: s crvusd em a ​ ( t ) ≤ 0.5 because additional crvusd inflows do not immediately threaten stable-side depletion in that region. however, once pools become crvusd-heavy: s crvusd em a ​ ( t ) > 0.5 the methodology linearly reduces the remaining capacity. the term: max ( 0 , s crvusd em a ​ ( t ) − 0.5 ) represents the excess crvusd inventory share above balance. as this quantity increases, stable-side liquidity declines and additional crvusd inflows become progressively more destabilizing. the framework therefore, estimates remaining marginal absorption capacity rather than total theoretical capacity. the implementation retrieves pool balances directly from the curve pool contracts, identifies crvusd by token address, computes pool-level imbalance and ema-smoothed imbalance, computes pool-level safe capacity, and aggregates capacity across all pegkeeper pools. gauge tvl is estimated as: t v l p k ​ = l p gauge ​ × v p where l p gauge ​ is the gauge lp token balance and v p is the pool virtual price. the implementation is shown in the accompanying script. limitations the current framework has three principal limitations. first, the safe crvusd fraction is an implicit proxy for peg safety rather than an explicit economic constraint. the parameter: f safe ​ = 0.70 assumes that pegkeeper pools can become crvusd-heavy up to this fraction while remaining within an acceptable peg-risk regime. however, peg risk is continuous rather than binary. a more direct formulation would define safety in terms of the pool-implied crvusd price: p crvusd ​ ( q , t ) ≥ p m i n ​ where q is additional crvusd inflow into pegkeeper pools and p m i n ​ is the lowest acceptable crvusd price. under this formulation, safe capacity would be defined as: c p k ​ ( t ) = max q s.t. p crvusd ​ ( q , t ) ≥ p m i n ​ this would replace the empirical safe-fraction assumption with an explicit price-impact constraint. second, the method models pegkeeper pools as the absorption sink for yb-originated crvusd sell pressure, but it does not model the state of the yb pools as the source of that pressure. the current implementation assumes a fixed stress multiplier: m y b ​ = 2.5 independent of yb pool composition. this is conservative but incomplete. if yb pools are crvusd-heavy, more crvusd sell pressure can originate from unwind activity. if yb pools are btc-heavy or crvusd-light, the potential crvusd sell pressure is mechanically lower. a more complete framework would make the multiplier state-dependent: m y b ​ ( t ) = g ( s crvusd,yb ​ ( t ) ) where s crvusd,yb ​ ( t ) denotes the crvusd inventory share in yb pools. the safe exposure ceiling would then be expressed as: s m a x ​ ( t ) = m y b ​ ( t ) c p k ​ ( t ) ​ rather than using a constant multiplier. in addition, the current stress multiplier should also be interpreted in light of the recent yieldbasis upgrade . the upgrade is intended to reduce pressure on crvusd by changing the yb pool mechanism, which implies that the mapping from yb exposure to pegkeeper sell pressure may decline after migration. therefore, m y b ​ should not be treated as a permanent structural constant, but as a conservative pre-upgrade stress parameter that should be recalibrated once post-upgrade pool data are available. third, the current state-dependent method assumes that remaining pegkeeper absorption capacity declines linearly with crvusd-heavy imbalance. in the implementation, the cap is computed as: s m a x ​ ( t ) = m y b ​ ⋅ [ f safe ​ max ( 0 , s crvusd em a ​ ( t ) − 0.5 ) ] ⋅ t v l p k ​ ( t ) this means that each additional percentage point of crvusd-heavy imbalance reduces remaining capacity by the same amount. this is a simplifying assumption. in practice, the relationship between pool imbalance, marginal slippage, and crvusd price pressure is likely nonlinear, especially as stable-side liquidity becomes depleted. a more robust framework would therefore estimate pegkeeper absorption capacity directly from the pool curve: c p k ​ ( t ) = max q s.t. δ p crvusd ​ ( q , t ) ≤ δ p m a x ​ and combine this with a state-dependent estimate of yb-originated sell pressure: s m a x ​ ( t ) = g ( s crvusd,yb ​ ( t ) ) c p k ​ ( t ) ​ taken together, the current model should be interpreted as a conservative, pool-state-aware heuristic. it improves on the static pegkeeper tvl heuristic by accounting for current pegkeeper imbalance, but it does not yet impose an explicit crvusd price constraint, account for yb-side source capacity, or model the nonlinear relationship between imbalance and marginal price impact. the script implements the linear pegkeeper-side imbalance adjustment only. llamarisk-authored title: Michael Meeting Notes 3/11/26
sourcePath: Handover Package/Miscellaneous/Michael Meeting Notes 3-slash-11-slash-26.html
excerpt: Meeting Summary Topic: Curve mechanics, LLAMMA/LlamaLend oracle design, liquidation behavior, liquidity requirements, and gold collateral opportunities Date: March 11, 2026 Participants: Michael Egorov, Wormhole Oracle, Zeki Blue,
searchText: michael meeting notes 3/11/26 miscellaneous meeting summary topic: curve mechanics, llamma/llamalend oracle design, liquidation behavior, liquidity requirements, and gold collateral opportunities date: march 11, 2026 participants: michael egorov, wormhole oracle, zeki blue, erdal tuncberk, xm3van purpose: internal knowledge transfer session to deepen understanding of curve protocol mechanics and extract risk-management principles grounded in protocol design. executive summary this session focused primarily on how llamma/llamalend should think about oracle construction, liquidation dynamics, external liquidity dependence, and collateral onboarding standards. michael’s core message was that safe risk management in llamalend cannot be reduced to static ltv or price-volatility assumptions alone. the system must be understood as a coupled mechanism involving: oracle smoothness band structure and liquidation behavior external market liquidity and arbitrage speed redemption latency / long-duration assumptions feedback loops between llamma and external venues a major theme was that smooth oracles are foundational to llamma safety . sudden oracle jumps can crystalize losses during soft liquidation and create behavior that is incompatible with how llamma values positions. this is why michael emphasized that raw chainlink-style jumpy feeds are generally a poor fit for llamalend , unless they are smoothed or replaced by pool-based oracles. a second major theme was that external liquidity capacity must be treated as a core risk parameter . if llamma inventory becomes materially larger than the external market’s ability to absorb price flow, the system can enter a reflexive selloff / “death spiral” dynamic, where llamma selling pushes external prices further, which then feeds back into the oracle and causes further llamma selling. the session also covered gold-backed assets as an attractive collateral class, but only if paired with an oracle design that avoids discontinuous price jumps. michael strongly favored curve pool / fxswap-based oracle approaches for gold over direct chainlink feed dependence. gold was framed as strong collateral in principle, but only when the market structure and oracle implementation are compatible with llamma’s mechanics. key takeaways 1. oracle smoothing is essential for llamma-compatible collateral michael’s view was that the specific smoothing method matters less than ensuring that some smoothing exists . he referenced existing code that can wrap an oracle and impose a cap on how fast pps / vault-rate-like components can move. oraclevaultwrapper: https://github.com/curvefi/curve-stablecoin/blob/master/curve_stablecoin/price_oracles/oraclevaultwrapper.vy main point for llamma-style lending, the oracle should not move discontinuously. even if the underlying asset is fundamentally sound, abrupt oracle updates can create realized losses during soft liquidation and hard liquidation accounting. implication for vault-like assets or redemption-rate-based assets, a practical safety improvement is to use an oracle wrapper that rate-limits price/pps updates . this is especially relevant for assets with donation/inflation-style attack surfaces or sudden valuation step changes. applied discussion the team discussed patching markets through an oracle proxy approach and specifically considered this for fxsave , which michael agreed could be prudent. his view was that even if a manipulation is not currently profitable due to the amount of supply sitting in pools, it is still wise to harden the design now in case the asset grows and the balance between pool liquidity and vault tvl changes later. 2. llamma v2-style manipulation is harder, but not irrelevant michael distinguished between easier attack classes and the more expensive manipulation problem in llamalend v2-like settings. main point manipulation becomes much harder if an attacker has to sustain it over hours rather than minutes. in that case, they would need to continuously pay trading fees and absorb slippage while arbitrage and natural market flow work against them. risk interpretation this means the system becomes significantly safer when the attack requires: a long maintenance window, meaningful fee expenditure, persistent suppression or distortion of a market price, and resistance against organic trader/arbitrage flow. practical lesson the right question is not “can the price be moved?” but rather: how long must it be moved, how expensive is that to sustain, and how much organic/arbitrage flow will resist it? that is a much more useful framework for assessing llamma oracle attackability than simply measuring instantaneous slippage. 3. why smooth oracles are necessary: llamma liquidation accounting assumes continuity michael gave an important conceptual explanation of why jumpy oracles are dangerous in llamalend. core mechanism in llamma, when a position is inside soft liquidation bands, the system effectively values the position under the assumption of smooth progression through the bands. if the oracle remains stable, inventory moved through llamma can in principle be traded back without introducing sudden valuation discontinuities. but if the oracle suddenly jumps, losses that were previously latent become realized. this happens because the position is now being evaluated against a different oracle anchor, while inventory has already been transformed along the prior liquidation path. why chainlink is problematic a chainlink feed can update in discrete jumps. llamma is not naturally built for this kind of discontinuous movement. michael explicitly stated this is why chainlink cannot simply be plugged in directly. risk consequence if the oracle can jump too quickly: soft liquidation may become more lossy, collateral protection degrades, and the protocol may no longer benefit from the intended gradual liquidation mechanics. this is one of the most important conceptual points from the session. 4. small-band positions near oracle price are more vulnerable michael noted a known sensitivity in positions that are concentrated very close to the oracle with very few bands. main point a position with only a very small number of bands near the oracle can be vulnerable to a two-block manipulation-style issue. he specifically noted that around four bands is the vulnerable region, while larger-band positions are safer. interpretation the danger is not just total leverage, but how tightly the position is packed around current oracle price. narrow, near-oracle configurations are more exposed to adverse effects from short-horizon price/oracle changes. risk-management implication when designing markets or simulation frameworks, risk analysis should explicitly consider: number of bands, distance from oracle, oracle ema behavior, and how small oracle changes propagate through narrow liquidation zones. this suggests that “safe ltv” cannot be divorced from band geometry. 5. redemption time and oracle timing must be analyzed together a recurring theme was that redemption time / arbitrage time / ema time must be aligned. michael emphasized that this is a tricky systems-design problem rather than a single-parameter decision. main point if llamma liquidity is very large, but on-chain liquidity is small and arbitrage is slow, then the oracle ema time needs to be chosen in relation to how quickly markets can actually arbitrage and redeem. if this is mismatched, the system can destabilize. michael’s warning if the oracle reacts faster than markets can absorb and correct the imbalance, the system can enter reflexive liquidation dynamics. he explicitly described the risk of a death spiral if oracle timing and arbitrage/redemption reality are not aligned. important implication for redeemable assets, wrapped assets, rwa-like assets, or assets relying on off-chain settlement: the appropriate oracle speed is not determined purely by price volatility, it is determined by the real-world latency of correction mechanisms . this is critical for assets like: wrapped btc variants, gold-backed tokens, rwas, or redemption-based synthetic instruments. simulation and monitoring discussion 6. continuous monitoring is useful, but not sufficient by itself the team described work underway to continuously run the llamma simulator and update risk views incrementally as on-chain parameters and conditions evolve. michael agreed this makes sense, particularly if it is computationally cheap and used to reassess risk after observed volatility events. however, he pushed back on the idea that continuous reruns alone provide deep predictive comfort. michael’s main caution historical calm is not enough. extreme risk often comes from events larger than any seen previously. therefore: continuous monitoring is useful for updating risk after new stress events, but it does not “solve” tail-risk prediction. best use of monitoring michael seemed most aligned with using monitoring to answer questions like: did a recent event reveal that current parameters were riskier than expected? should parameter assumptions be revised after a new high-volatility episode? has market structure changed enough to warrant adjusting limits? internal takeaway continuous monitoring is valuable as a parameter review and anomaly detection tool , not as a guarantee that future tail events are already captured. 7. current llamma simulation should ideally be coupled with pool simulation michael identified an important limitation in standalone llamma simulation: it may not model the effect of llamma activity on the external market price itself. problem if the simulator treats the price path as exogenous, it can miss the feedback loop where: llamma sells into an external market, external market price moves more because liquidity is thin, oracle ema follows that price, bands shift, llamma sells more, the cycle accelerates. why this matters this is precisely the mechanism of the death spiral he described. it is not enough to simulate llamma against historical prices if llamma could itself materially affect the realized external execution path. recommendation implied by michael a better framework would couple: llamma inventory dynamics, pool liquidity dynamics, oracle ema behavior, and arbitrage replenishment assumptions. in short, llamma and the reference market should be modeled jointly where possible. external liquidity and debt ceiling design 8. core risk rule: external liquidity density must not be inferior to llamma pressure michael provided one of the strongest risk heuristics of the discussion. concept compare how much notional must be bought or sold to move price by 1% in: external markets, versus llamma. if llamma contains more effective liquidity pressure than the market can absorb, that is an alarm condition. framing he described llamma as behaving somewhat like an “anti-uniswap v3,” while uniswap v3 and similar external venues provide the opposing inventory. if both sides have comparable liquidity density across the relevant price interval, they can offset each other and avoid spiral dynamics. practical formulation a useful risk metric is: usd notional required to move price by 1% externally versus usd notional llamma can unload over the corresponding soft-liquidation range if llamma’s effective sell pressure exceeds the external market’s depth, risk rises materially. michael’s conclusion this is something that does require continuous monitoring and should directly influence market limits. that is a major point: debt ceilings should be informed by liquidity-density comparisons, not only by volatility or market cap. 9. off-chain liquidity and arbitrage matter; on-chain-only analysis is incomplete when the team described frameworks based on aggregator quotes and observed on-chain depth curves, michael noted that this is useful but still incomplete because actual absorbency also depends on: off-chain liquidity, centralized exchange depth, and arbitrage traders connecting those venues back to on-chain markets. implication a purely on-chain debt ceiling model may be too conservative for some assets and too optimistic for others, depending on how reliable off-chain arbitrage is during stress. best interpretation the right framework should treat observed on-chain depth as the visible core, then layer in assumptions about: replenishment speed, cross-venue arbitrage reliability, stress-state depth contraction, and whether off-chain liquidity can truly be mobilized under market stress. this aligns with the team’s effort to use historical quote data and stressed-state depth curves, but michael’s point is that those assumptions must remain explicit and challengeable. asset onboarding framework 10. assets with weak native liquidity can still work if redemption into deep liquidity exists michael made an important nuance: an asset does not necessarily need deep standalone liquidity if it can reliably redeem into something that does. however if that is the case, the asset’s: ema time, health evaluation horizon, and borrowing limits must be adapted to that redemption reality. example logic for a wrapped asset redeemable into a highly liquid base asset: the wrapper itself may not need huge spot-market depth, but the protocol must account for the time and reliability of redemption, and the oracle must not react in a way that outruns that redemption path. this is especially relevant to: wrapped btc assets, tokenized gold, rwas, or other representations whose value depends on conversion to a deeper underlying market. 11. but wrapper failure risk creates a competing requirement for faster oracle response michael used a wrapped btc example to show that longer ema smoothing is not always better. tension a long ema helps protect against reflexive spirals driven by thin liquidity and slow arbitrage. but a long ema also delays the protocol’s response if the wrapped asset itself fails, depegs, or is hacked. example he referenced a btc wrapper that had historically traded far below btc after an incident, illustrating that wrapper failure is not hypothetical. risk lesson there is an unavoidable tradeoff: longer ema protects against transient market dislocations and slow-arbitrage feedback loops. shorter ema protects against genuine collateral impairment. this means oracle design must be asset-specific. there is no universal “safe ema.” gold discussion 12. gold was viewed as highly attractive collateral in principle there was broad alignment in the conversation that gold-backed assets are attractive for curve and llamalend. why gold is attractive relatively low correlation to crypto, diversification benefit, generally strong collateral quality, and clear potential user demand. michael described gold as “excellent collateral.” 13. gold’s main challenge is oracle design, not collateral concept the major issue is not whether gold is fundamentally good collateral, but whether the oracle structure is compatible with llamma. problem with chainlink-style gold feeds michael highlighted that chainlink gold feeds can have: material deviation thresholds, discrete updates, and scheduled downtime / non-24/7 behavior. this is problematic for llamma because sudden oracle jumps can cause losses during soft liquidation. the discussion referenced: approximately 0.3% deviation threshold for one gold feed, and approximately 0.5% deviation threshold for paxos gold-related feed behavior. michael’s view was that these thresholds are not trivial in llamma terms and should be explicitly simulated. key takeaway for gold collateral, a pool-based, smooth oracle is much more attractive than a discrete off-chain feed. 14. preferred approach: gold pool / fxswap-backed oracle michael strongly favored supporting gold through: a curve gold/usd pool, or an fxswap-style structure, and using that market as the basis for a smoother oracle. why this would provide: smoother price discovery, llamma-compatible oracle behavior, and stronger integration between lending market design and market microstructure. he specifically said fxswap would be a perfect fit for gold. strategic implication if curve wants gold in lending or mint markets, building the supporting market structure first may be the right sequence: establish gold/usd liquidity on curve, generate a smooth market-based oracle, then onboard the collateral into lending. this is much safer than onboarding gold collateral first and trying to rely on a jumpy external feed. 15. gold pool subsidy requirements likely appear manageable michael’s rough view was that a $1m-sized pool is not especially hard to achieve, and that several percent apr in subsidy may be enough to support viable concentrated liquidity, though he stressed that proper simulation is needed. important nuance the subsidy cost may not be fully “lost,” because: some subsidized rebalancing spend is recovered through lp apr, and if genuine on-chain trading demand is strong, organic fees can eventually offset or even surpass the subsidy requirement. strategic message a gold pool could begin subsidy-assisted, then potentially reduce reliance on subsidy if volume becomes self-sustaining. crvusd pool attractiveness and fee policy 16. reducing admin fees on crvusd pools may help attract issuers, but needs market validation the team raised the idea, apparently from curve-side discussion earlier in the day, of reducing admin fees on crvusd pools to make them more attractive for issuers. michael’s view this is plausible in principle, but should be validated directly with issuers. the key question is whether the fee reduction is meaningful enough to change issuer preference or lp economics. implication this is a business-development and market-structure lever, but it should not be assumed to work automatically. the relevant question is whether the admin-fee burden is actually a decisive constraint for issuers considering crvusd-paired pools. recommended internal interpretation 17. the meeting’s central risk philosophy the strongest overall lesson from michael is that good llamalend risk management is systems thinking . you cannot assess a market by looking only at: collateral volatility, or debt ceiling, or feed type, or liquidity depth, or ltv. instead, you must analyze the interaction among: oracle continuity, llamma band structure, external liquidity density, arbitrage/replenishment speed, redemption latency, and wrapper failure risk. that is the real risk surface. concrete action items high priority 1. build/expand oracle wrapper framework for vault/pps-style assets internalize the use of smoothing / rate-limiting wrappers for: vault-rate components, redemption-rate components, pps-like values, and potentially existing markets where future growth could expose dormant attack surfaces. fxsave was specifically validated as a reasonable candidate for precautionary hardening. 2. extend simulation to include coupled pool dynamics where possible the current simulator framework is useful, but the most important missing piece is the endogenous feedback loop between llamma and external market pricing. we should prioritize frameworks that approximate: pool slippage under llamma-driven execution, ema follow-through, recursive band migration, and arbitrage replenishment assumptions. 3. incorporate liquidity-density-based debt ceiling logic debt ceiling recommendations should explicitly incorporate: external usd depth per 1% move, llamma sell pressure over the relevant band interval, and alarms when llamma inventory materially exceeds market absorbency. 4. asset onboarding framework should explicitly include redemption-time / ema-time matching for wrapper and rwa-style assets, add a formal framework assessing: redemption latency, liquidity source quality, arbitrage speed, wrapper failure scenarios, and whether long ema / short ema tradeoffs are acceptable. gold-specific 5. prioritize the gold market structure thesis there appears to be strong alignment that gold is an attractive direction for curve. internal research should focus on: curve gold/usd pool feasibility, fxswap structure for gold, subsidy sizing, oracle quality comparison between pool-based and chainlink-based approaches, and llamma loss simulation under discrete feed jumps. 6. simulate chainlink gold feed behavior inside llamalend run explicit simulations comparing: smooth pool oracle, raw chainlink-like update process, and potentially smoothed chainlink wrapper approaches, to quantify soft-liquidation loss behavior and validate whether any feed-only design is viable. 7. coordinate ecosystem outreach given michael’s indication that tether may be interested in pushing gold on-chain, there may be a practical path to seed liquidity or subsidy support for a gold pair. this should be followed up from a business-development angle alongside technical market design work. suggested internal principles to carry forward principle 1 a collateral is not safe just because it is fundamentally sound. it also needs the right oracle shape and sufficient absorbent market structure. principle 2 smoothness matters as much as accuracy for llamma oracles. a precise oracle that jumps can be worse than a slightly lagged oracle that moves continuously. principle 3 debt ceilings should scale with executable liquidity, not just market size. the relevant question is whether the external market can absorb llamma flow without destabilizing feedback. principle 4 ema time is a risk tradeoff, not a free safety knob. longer ema protects against transient dislocations, but slower response can be dangerous if collateral impairment is real. principle 5 gold looks strategically attractive for curve, but only if supported by native curve liquidity and oracle architecture. bottom line this meeting materially reinforced that llamma risk management is inseparable from oracle design and market microstructure. michael’s guidance points toward a more mature framework where market safety is evaluated not just through static collateral parameters, but through a dynamic understanding of how liquidation bands, smooth oracle behavior, arbitrage timing, redemption frictions, and external liquidity interact. the clearest immediate strategic opportunity discussed was gold , but the clearest broader protocol lesson was this: for llamalend, the safest market is not simply the one with “good collateral.” it is the one where oracle motion, liquidation mechanics, and executable market depth are all aligned.
