title: CRV-long LlamaLend Recovery Pool Analysis
sourcePath: Handover Package/Operational State/Impaired Markets/CRV-long LlamaLend Recovery Pool Analysis.html
excerpt: 1. Purpose and objectives The CRV-long LlamaLend market carries roughly $705K of bad debt: loans where the CRV collateral is worth less than the crvUSD owed, leaving the vault's lenders holding shares ( cvcrvUSD ) that can't be re
searchText: crv-long llamalend recovery pool analysis operational state impaired markets 1. purpose and objectives the crv-long llamalend market carries roughly $705k of bad debt: loans where the crv collateral is worth less than the crvusd owed, leaving the vault's lenders holding shares ( cvcrvusd ) that can't be redeemed at face. before april this debt had no path to resolution other than waiting for crv to recover on its own. michwill proposed a free-market alternative in crv-long llamalend market recovery : a small curve pool that trades the impaired vault share against crvusd, priced through a rate oracle pinned at pricepershare / √2 (a ~29.3% floor discount). the pool lets anyone buy the share cheaply and then run an atomic liquidation that pays down a bad loan and redeems the share back out of the vault. if the share was bought cheaply enough, the trade clears a profit. the mechanism doesn't erase the loss. it makes paying it down a rational trade for outside capital instead of a charity nobody volunteers for. the proposal frames this as "a recovery method with an option-like payoff, working as an investment for everyone who wants to participate." the dao is invited but not required. the only thing it asked of governance was a gauge so the pool's liquidity providers could earn crv emissions. by construction the whole thing is permissionless and runs without ongoing intervention once the gauge is set, which is a useful property rather than a goal in itself. the design was put forward against two earlier-discussed alternatives that both spend protocol money directly: a direct treasury repayment of the bad debt ( temp check: use treasury funds to repay bad debt ), and the compensation-grant precedent from the vyper exploit ( proposal to recompensate lps affected by curve pool exploit ). this report has two jobs. first, with the pool live for about six weeks and the gauge now weighted, check whether each thing the design set out to do is actually happening. second, judge whether the approach is a viable, repeatable way to recover bad debt, specifically whether it can scale to the other impaired llamalend markets, which together carry roughly $1.22m more. the first is a goal-by-goal audit; the second is the question that decides whether this is a one-off fix or a template. 2. how the pool is doing so far headline value read bad debt (live oracle mark) $705,195 down from a $757,509 peak at launch shortfall paid down by liquidators $52,314 across 36 liquidations of one borrower pool tvl ~$460k from ~$198 at launch, once emissions turned on crv emissions to the gauge $109,635/yr ~0.45% gauge weight, ~23.9% apr on tvl emissions spent so far ~$8,412 over the six-week window trading fees earned so far ~$2,900 1% swap fee, fee/emissions ratio ~0.34 lenders who took a cash exit 2 at a 35.6% realized discount to face liquidator gross profit ~$55,675 $183.5k redeemed minus $127.8k spent vault backing per share ~77% up from a lower trough as debt grinds down the weekly picture below shows the two phases plainly: emissions and depth were near zero for the first stretch, then the gauge weight kicked in and tvl climbed past $400k. trading volume and fees stayed thin and spiky, riding on a single liquidator bot rather than steady flow. weekly emissions, tvl, volume, and fees bad-debt trajectory 3. the goals the pool aims to: give stuck lenders a real exit, at a transparent discount. reduce the bad debt by making liquidation profitable enough that it actually gets paid down. fund deep pool liquidity through crv emissions, enough yield to keep lps in, at far lower cost to the dao than a direct buyout. open an option-like bet on crv recovery to outside capital. 4. goal-by-goal assessment 1. a real exit for stuck lenders two lenders have sold into the pool. they received $6,172 against $9,579 of face owed, a 35.6% realized discount. that's a touch worse than the 29.3% floor the rate oracle is supposed to guarantee, because the pool was leaning share-heavy when they sold, which pushes the price below the floor. a larger exit can move the price hard, but the number that matters to a lender is what they lose against face value. a simulated $50k sell-down costs about 5.8% in slippage against spot now, down from 98% before emissions deepened the pool. slippage against spot flatters the picture, though, because spot already trades well below face. measured against face value, that same $50k exit is about a 38.5% haircut, and it has barely improved as the pool deepened, because roughly 29.3% of it is the structural √2 floor that depth can't remove. the chart shows both lines: slippage-vs-spot falls toward zero while discount-vs-face plateaus near 38%, and the gap between them is the floor. so the venue exists and the depth is real, but a lender still walks away about 38% below face. adoption is tiny regardless. most lenders are still holding. $50k exit: discount vs face and slippage vs spot 2. reduce the bad debt of 36 liquidations, 35 ran the full atomic recipe in a single transaction: flash-borrow crvusd, buy the cheap share, liquidate the loan, redeem the share, repay the flash loan, keep the spread. liquidators paid $52,314 of shortfall they would never have paid voluntarily, and walked away with roughly $55,675 gross before gas. the arbitrage is live and profitable, which is exactly the behavior the design needed to manufacture. cumulative shortfall paid by liquidators across the 36 events on the protocol's balance sheet that shows up as a real dent. the live bad-debt mark fell from $757,509 to $705,195, and the $52k of improvement matches the shortfall the liquidators paid almost exactly, the clean signal that the pool, not a crv price move, is what bent the curve. per-share backing recovered to about 77%. however every other position is too deep to be profitable. of the $705k still outstanding, almost every position is missing 40 to 55% of its backing, while a liquidator only earns about 30 to 35% on the share discount, so the loss to close them outweighs the gain. none have been touched at today's crv price, and the bad debt stopped falling the moment that one borrower was exhausted. shortfall/debt for every position vs the arb-profitability ceiling so the curve didn't bend a little and keep going. it bent once, by the size of the single solvent position, and flattened. at constant crv the bad debt sits at ~$705k and backing holds near 77%, not climbing toward 100%. the remaining 93% waits on a crv recovery, not on more time. 4. emissions subsidy: deep pool, cheap for the dao the emissions do two jobs at once; they pay lps about 23.9% apr, and that yield pulled tvl from nothing to ~$460k. the pool is deep because the reward is attractive. they are also the dao's entire cost. a direct buyout would cost the dao a dollar for every dollar of bad debt retired. this route has so far spent $8,412 of emissions against $52,314 of bad debt retired, about $0.16 of subsidy per dollar cleared. the emissions don't pay the shortfall. liquidators pay it, funded by the discount that exiting lenders accept. the emissions only rent the pool depth that makes the arbitrage liquid. so the $0.16 is the dao's subsidy cost per dollar cleared, and it's low precisely because the principal cost has been pushed onto arbitrageurs and the lenders who sell cheap. fees have covered only about 34% of the emissions bill over the window, and in most weeks far less. the pool came closest to paying for itself during one volume spike, when fees reached 88% of that week's emissions, then fell back below 10%. cumulative fees vs crv emissions, and the weekly fees/emissions ratio 5. a long call option-like bet for outside capital the design allows outside capital to take a speculative position: buy the vault share at a discount, keep the floor value on the downside, and keep the upside if crv climbs back toward the $0.96–$1.24 band where shares redeem at full face. on the liquidity side, the bet is clearly populated: about 93% of pool tvl comes from addresses that aren't stuck lenders. on the share-holding side, the data is unambiguous. about 162 million shares have been bought out of the pool, roughly $203k of face value, and almost all of it was round-tripped straight back out by the arbitrage bot in the same transaction. once you strip out those round-trips and any shares re-deposited as pool liquidity, what's left genuinely held in a wallet is 130,000 shares, about $163 of face value, spread across six addresses . that's 0.08% of everything bought. nobody is holding the share as a standing option in any size that matters. so the design's speculation venue exists in the form people will actually use, which is providing liquidity for the emissions yield. however the pool is carried by yield-farming lps and the arbitrage bot, not by option-holders. 5. what to expect, holding crv price and vote weight constant hold crv near $0.21 and the gauge weight near 0.45%, and the headline is short: the arbitrage has essentially already done what it can. the tempting move is to read the $52k retired so far as a pace and extrapolate it to a full clear in about a year. that would be wrong, and goal 2 shows why. the bot didn't clear $52k and keep going. it cleared the one position whose shortfall sat inside the pool discount, ground it to dust, and ran out of profitable targets. there is no pace to carry forward. bad debt stalls near $705k. the ~$52k already retired is close to the whole of what the arb can reach at this price. the remaining 93% sits in positions too deep to liquidate at a profit, so absent a crv move the bad-debt mark holds around $705k and per-share backing holds near 77%. it does not grind to zero. the cheap part is over, but the meter keeps running. on the slice it cleared the mechanism was efficient: about $8,412 of emissions against $52,314 retired, roughly $0.16 of subsidy per dollar, far under the dollar-for-dollar a direct buyout costs. that efficiency does not extend, because there is nothing left for it to clear cheaply. meanwhile the dao keeps paying ~$110k a year in emissions for a pool whose liquidation engine has stalled. the spend still buys something real, just narrower than "recovery": standing exit liquidity for any lender who wants out, at the ~38% haircut to face from goal 1, plus a live venue for the crv-recovery option. lenders mostly just wait. with the grind stalled, a holder's backing sits near 77% rather than climbing toward 100%. the only way to turn a position into cash is to sell into the pool at the ~38% discount, which two lenders have done. everyone else holds an impaired claim whose value now moves with the crv price, not with liquidator activity. the remaining 93% is a one-sided crv-price bet. the bad debt's exposure to crv is asymmetric, which is the one piece of good news. on the downside there is little left to lose: these positions are already soft-liquidated through their llamma bands, so what backs them is crvusd now, not crv, and a further fall in crv barely moves the number. on the upside there is real optionality. if crv climbs back toward the $0.957 to $1.242 band that michwill's recovery analysis marks out in the proposal , the soft-liquidation reverses, the collateral reconverts to crv at higher value, and those deep positions become solvent and liquidatable on their own. so the constant-price case is the floor of a one-sided bet: the hole can't get much deeper, and only a crv recovery fills it. with crv at $0.21 against a band that starts at $0.957, that recovery is far off and entirely exogenous to the mechanism. 6. can it scale to the other markets? this is the question that decides whether the recovery pool is a one-off patch or a repeatable tool. the other impaired llamalend markets carry roughly $1.22m of bad debt between them, on top of this market's ~$705k. the cash cost of copying the mechanism is not the binding constraint, because the dao never pays the principal; liquidators and exiting lenders do. what the dao spends is gauge weight, and that is the scarce resource. this market uses about 0.45% of weekly crv emissions to keep ~$705k of debt liquid. covering the other markets at a similar ratio would take roughly another 0.35% of total weight. in cash terms that's cheap. in governance terms it's contested, because every basis point of weight is taken from some other gauge that wants it, and the affected lenders don't control the vote. but this market exposed a limit more fundamental than the vote. the arb only reaches debt whose shortfall is shallower than the pool discount, and in the crv market that turned out to be a single position, about 7% of the hole. the other 93% was too deeply underwater to touch at all. so the question that decides whether the mechanism helps a given market isn't its total bad debt, or even its vote cost. it's how much of that debt sits below the discount ceiling. a market whose loans are mostly deep underwater gets almost nothing from this, no matter how much emissions it's handed. the rented-depth warning still applies on top: each new market carries its own ongoing emissions bill, not a one-time grant. so the honest read on scalability: the cash cost is trivial, but the mechanism only recovers the shallow, nearly-solvent slice of each market's bad debt. for the deep majority it offers a discounted exit and a standing option on price, not a recovery. whether a gauge per market is worth it depends on how much of that market is shallow enough to clear, and on a vote that competes with everything else for emissions. it's a narrow tool, not a general one. 7. bottom line the pool does the hard part it was designed for. it turns an unworkable loss into a profitable trade, and on the one position where that trade was solvent it cleared ~$52k of bad debt for about $8k of emissions, a fifth of what a buyout would cost. lps showed up for the yield and made the pool genuinely deep. but the reach is narrow, and that's the real finding. that $52k is about 7% of the hole, and it's most of what the arb can touch: the other 93% sits in positions too deeply underwater to liquidate at a profit, so at today's crv price the cleanup has stalled, not slowed. the other goals are thin too. lenders have no real cash exit, two have used it at a ~38% haircut to face. the option-style speculation didn't materialize; the pool runs on yield-farming lps and one arbitrage bot, not on people holding the recovery bet. and the depth is rented: fees cover about a third of the emissions, so the dao keeps paying ~$110k a year to keep a stalled engine warm. the rest of the bad debt, here and across the other markets, isn't waiting on time or on more liquidators. it's waiting on crv to recover, which the mechanism can't manufacture.

title: LlamaLend Bad-Debt Remediation
sourcePath: Handover Package/Operational State/Impaired Markets/LlamaLend Bad-Debt Remediation.html
excerpt: Summary The LlamaLend v1 markets carrying bad debt — loans whose collateral is worth less than the crvUSD owed, leaving the affected lenders holding vault shares that cannot be redeemed at face value. This spans roughly a dozen ma
searchText: llamalend bad-debt remediation operational state impaired markets summary the llamalend v1 markets carrying bad debt — loans whose collateral is worth less than the crvusd owed, leaving the affected lenders holding vault shares that cannot be redeemed at face value. this spans roughly a dozen markets across ethereum, arbitrum, fraxtal, optimism, and sonic, ≈$1.18m of shortfall in aggregate. these markets are being deprecated ahead of llamalend v2. deprecation freezes the shortfall — it stops interest from deepening it and prevents new exposure — but it does not resolve the existing loss. resolving that loss is a distinct workstream and the subject of this document. introduction the affected markets are llamalend lend markets, where the borrowable liquidity comes from third-party depositors rather than from crvusd itself, so those depositors bear any shortfall. the largest case, the crv-collateral market, took on its bad debt during a single sharp collateral drawdown. curve's soft-liquidation mechanism (llamma) gradually converts a position's collateral into crvusd as the collateral price falls; once that conversion is complete and the resulting crvusd still falls short of the debt, the residual is a realized shortfall borne by the market's lenders, who can no longer withdraw at face value. in aggregate the shortfall is roughly $1.18m across about thirteen markets on ethereum, arbitrum, fraxtal, optimism, and sonic, and it is highly concentrated: the crv-collateral market alone accounts for about $705k, close to 60% of the total, while a long tail of markets carry only sub-five-figure "dust" amounts. each affected lender claim is already tokenised as an erc-4626 vault share, so every impaired market's loss is a discrete, transferable object that can be priced or redeemed. two things are already in motion independently of any remediation decision. first, the markets are being wound down ahead of llamalend v2: each has its borrow rate set to roughly 0% (so interest stops deepening the shortfall), its loan discount raised toward the contract maximum, its listing removed from the user interface, and its market gauge retired. these containment steps freeze the shortfall but do not resolve it the 0% rate in particular cuts both ways: it stops interest from deepening the hole, but it also removes any carrying cost for borrowers, so the underwater loans sit frozen at no cost and solvent borrowers have no incentive to repay and free up lender capital at face. second, a market-based recovery pool is already operating on the crv market: a curve stableswap pool trades the impaired vault share against crvusd at a structural discount (≈√2, about 29.3% below face), so liquidators can buy shares cheaply, run atomic liquidations that pay down bad loans, and redeem the shares — turning the shortfall into a rational trade rather than a donation. its behaviour to date informs, but does not bind, the choices for the other markets. how to read the problem the loss is already realised: short of a genuine collateral-price recovery, nothing makes the hole disappear, so the suggested pathways differ mainly in who bears the loss and when, and at what discount, lenders exit. because an impaired position's collateral has already been converted to crvusd, the remaining claim behaves like an option on the collateral price, with a floor set by the crvusd already banked and upside only if the price climbs back into a defined band; below that band every mechanism here buys exit liquidity or containment, not principal recovery, and the recoverable portion stays tied to a price no one here controls. this property allowed an innovative recovery pool solution to be deployed for the crv market which is discussed further in this report. the loss still has to land somewhere: on the last lenders left in the market, on all current lenders pro-rata (socialisation), on the borrowers (through rate or liquidation pressure), or on the dao and its tokenholders (a funded intervention), each split carrying its own fairness argument that reasonable people weigh differently. it also helps to separate three goals that are easily conflated: recovery (reducing the shortfall, which needs price recovery or outside capital), exit liquidity (letting trapped lenders cash out at a transparent discount without shrinking the aggregate loss), and containment (stopping the shortfall from growing). markets in scope the table below joins curve's bad-debt and lending-markets endpoints chain market bad debt market tvl ethereum crv-long $705,184 $6,227,818 fraxtal fxs-long $145,857 $161,567 fraxtal squid-long $131,995 $137,763 arbitrum dlcbtc-long $81,683 $82,076 ethereum uwu-long $51,513 $54,173 arbitrum fxn-long $27,413 $27,888 arbitrum arb-long2 $19,614 $76,881 ethereum sdola-long2 $6,728 $437,627 optimism op-long $5,870 $7,665 optimism crv-long $391 $5,704 arbitrum weth-long $352 $121,494 sonic ws-long $109 $269 total $1,176,769 remediation pathways 5.1 covered via dao these routes resolve the shortfall by committing protocol resources — cash, a vesting governance-token grant, diverted revenue, emissions or stranded fees. they differ mainly in the form and timing of the cost. the main issue with this route is that dao simply doesn’t have enough funds to cover all bad debt at the same time. 5.1.1 recovery pool this solution involves a stableswap pool trading the impaired vault share against crvusd at a structural discount (≈√2, about 29.3% below face); liquidators arbitrage-buy shares and pay down bad loans, then redeem. a gauge-weight vote is executed for emissions to attract lp depth, which is a cost to the dao. we have provided an extensive analysis on the recovery pool and it’s performance . the result of our analysis suggests that as an innovative solution, recovery pool has potential to be applied for certain markets but not as a standalone solution to all markets with bad debt. to asses feasibility we scanned all market building upon michwill’s methodolgy as described below. methodology a recovery pool only helps a market if liquidators can profitably clear its bad debt. michwill's design ( crv-long llamalend market recovery ) prices the impaired vault share at a structural discount (≈√2, about 29.3% below face), so a liquidation profits only when the discount it captures beats the position's shortfall fraction: profitable ( i ) ⟺ debt i ​ shortfall i ​ ​ < d ( d ≈ 29.3% 2 ​ floor , ∼ 35% when share-heavy ) the market-level metric is the reachable shortfall fraction (rsf) : the share of a market's hole that liquidators can clear at today's price. rsf ( d ) = i ∑ ​ shortfall i ​ i : shortfall i ​ / debt i ​ < d ∑ ​ shortfall i ​ ​ pull every impaired llamalend market live from curve's bad-debt endpoint and compute its aggregate shortfall / debt. where the on-chain per-position scan is available, rsf and the full rsf(d) curve are computed directly. we ported michwill's llamma band revaluation from his published scripts (analyze_bad_debt.py, lp_price_vs_crv_price.py): read each position's bands, recover the band invariant y0, and re-value at any price with xy_at_price. this reconstructs each market's shortfall to the dollar against the live api. results only sdola-long2 (~$6.7k) and weth-long (~$352) fall inside the reachable band. every market with material bad debt sits above the ~30–35% discount ceiling, so 99.4% of all llamalend bad debt is unreachable at today's prices. the solution still has potential for future cases of bad debt. 5.1.2 direct repayment the dao can repay the shortfall directly, in full or in part. a full make-whole clears the entire hole and returns lenders to face, paid in cash or as a pro-rata governance-token grant on a vesting schedule. it is the cleanest exit for lenders, but the cash form is the largest single outlay; the vested-token form spreads the treasury impact yet ties the payout to a token-denominated value that may over- or under-compensate against the dollar loss; and either form raises moral-hazard and treasury-capacity questions. a targeted paydown is the other variant: repay only enough of the worst positions to pull them back into a liquidatable range, then let normal liquidation finish the job. it is far less costly than a full repayment and benefits from how concentrated the debt is, though it remains a direct outlay and a partial bailout — a targeted ≈$100k paydown was costed for the crv market. neither route needs a fresh outlay or token dilution if it is funded from resources the protocol has already earned. the clearest candidate is unclaimed layer-2 fees — protocol fees that have accrued but sit undistributed or stranded on layer-2s, which could be redirected toward either repayment. a more strategic option could be investing the layer2 fees and paying with the yield generated. 5.2 mint and lend crvusd into the pool lend crvusd equal to the shortfall into the market so trapped lenders can withdraw, to be recovered as the position normalises.provides exit without a permanent write-off; ties up capital indefinitely if recovery never comes, and the loan sits against an impaired book. 5.3 rate and parameter levers adjusting the market's interest rate or risk parameters can manufacture exits without the dao paying anything; the cost lands on borrowers and on incoming lenders rather than the treasury. the gentlest form is a free-floating rate — let the borrow rate float so that high utilisation drives a high rate, which attracts fresh lenders and gives existing lenders a path to exit while the market keeps operating. it is market-set and arguably even-handed, but it grows the nominal shortfall over time and relies on new lenders being willing to enter a known bad-debt market. a more aggressive form applies sustained rate or parameter pressure to force solvent borrowers out, freeing face-value exit for some lenders. that is directly contested on fairness — borrowers accepted different terms, the loss allocation shifts toward them and a forced-out borrower effectively received an interest-free loan — and borrowers may simply wait it out. neither has an established precedent. a forward-looking backstop: insurance / staked vault the routes above all address the existing shortfall. looking ahead, the dao could also build a standing backstop so future bad-debt events are absorbed automatically rather than handled case by case. one design is an opt-in, tranched savings-crvusd (scrvusd) vault: plain depositors keep the base yield with no bad-debt exposure, while depositors who opt into a junior "protection" tranche accept slashable principal in exchange for a higher yield. the slashable capital backstops any shortfall, and the yield premium is the price paid for that insurance. this is mainly forward-looking. precedents include aave's umbrella (a staked-atoken safety module that auto-covers deficits) and its earlier stkaave safety module, alongside senior/junior tranched credit vaults.

title: sDOLA LlamaLend Market — Post-Mortem v3
sourcePath: Handover Package/Operational State/Impaired Markets/sDOLA LlamaLend Market — Post-Mortem v3.html
excerpt: 1. Executive Summary On March 2, 2026, an attacker exploited the sDOLA/crvUSD LlamaLend market using a two-pronged flash loan attack, hard-liquidating 27 of 30 active borrowers (~$10.9M debt liquidated). The attack combined a larg
searchText: sdola llamalend market — post-mortem v3 operational state impaired markets 1. executive summary on march 2, 2026, an attacker exploited the sdola/crvusd llamalend market using a two-pronged flash loan attack, hard-liquidating 27 of 30 active borrowers (~$10.9m debt liquidated). the attack combined a large exchange on the llamma amm to force all positions into soft-liquidation, followed by a dolasavings.stake() call to inflate the sdola oracle price by ~13.8% — making the soft-liquidated positions instantly unhealthy. 2. attack overview tx 0xb93506af8f1a39f6a31e2d34f5f6a262c2799fef6e338640f42ab8737ed3d8a4 block 24,566,937 (march 2, 2026 ~04:00 utc) attacker 0x33a0aab2642c78729873786e5903cc30f9a94be2 via contract 0xd8e8544e0c808641b9b89dfb285b5655bd5b6982 flash loan 10m usdc + 15,986 weth (~$46m from morpho) market sdola/crvusd (controller: 0xad444663c6c92b497225c6ce65fee2e7f78bfb86 , amm: 0x0079885e248b572cdc4559a8b156745e2d8ea1f7 ) victims 27 of 30 borrowers hard-liquidated (3 survived with health >27%) pre-attack health 1.0%–19.5% for liquidated positions; 27%–91% for survivors timeline flash borrow $46m from morpho convert to crvusd via multiple routes (frax, alusd, weth collateral) exchange 13.25m crvusd into llamma — buy 9.83m sdola, traversing all bands redeem 10.6m sdola → 12.6m dola from vault — burns shares, collapsing sdola totalsupply from 11.77m to 1.16m dolasavings.stake(190k dola, sdola_address) — inflate oracle (190k against only 1.16m remaining shares = ~16% pps increase) hard-liquidate 27 of 30 positions (3 with health >27% survived) re-deposit into llamma, borrow 10.9m crvusd at inflated oracle (undercollateralized position) unwind all positions, repay flash loan 3. oracle architecture the sdola market uses a cryptofrompoolvaultwagg oracle ( 0x88822ee517bfe9a1b97bf200b0b6d3f356488ff2 ): price = pool.price_oracle() vault.converttoassets ( 1 0 18 ) × agg.price() ​ where: vault = sdola ( 0xb45ad160634c528cc3d2926d9807104fa3157305 ) — erc4626 wrapper around dolasavings pool = dola/crvusd stableswap ( 0xff17dab22f1e61078aba2623c89ce6110e878b3c ) — provides dola/crvusd ema price agg = crvusd aggregated price oracle ( 0x18672b1b0c623a30089a280ed9256379fb0e4e62 ) the pool's price_oracle() uses an internal ema (smoothed). but converttoassets() is read instantaneously — no smoothing, no twap. this is the vulnerability surface. the oracle contract's own source code warns: "only suitable for vaults which cannot be affected by donation attack (like sfrax)" 4. attack mechanism neither vector works alone. both are required. step 1: exchange on llamma (force soft-liquidation) the attacker calls amm.exchange(0, 1, 13.25m, 0) — selling 13.25m crvusd into the amm for 9.83m sdola. this traverses all occupied bands, converting borrowers' sdola collateral into crvusd within the bands. exchange() is permissionless with no oracle guard ( amm.vy l993 ). the only check is slippage ( min_amount ), which the attacker sets to 0. under normal conditions, no rational actor would push price far from oracle because the swap is unprofitable. the attacker doesn't care — profit comes from liquidations. exchange alone does not make any position liquidatable. health actually improves for most positions because the amm now holds more crvusd. the purpose of this step is to set up the precondition: all positions must be in soft-liquidation for step 2 to be effective. step 2: oracle inflation via stake() the sdola vault ( 0xb45ad160634c528cc3d2926d9807104fa3157305 ) computes totalassets() as: function totalassets() public view override returns (uint) { uint actualassets = savings.balanceof(address(this)) - remaininglastrevenue - weeklyrevenue[week]; return actualassets; } where savings.balanceof() is an internal accounting variable in dolasavings ( 0xe5f24791e273cb96a1f8e5b67bc2397f0ad9b8b4 ) — it only changes via stake() and unstake() . the attacker calls dolasavings.stake(190_000e18, sdola_address) . this: increases savings.balanceof(sdola) by 190k does not mint any sdola shares therefore inflates converttoassets() = totalassets / totalsupply note: a raw dola transfer to dolasavings does nothing — it wouldn't update the internal balanceof mapping. the attacker must call stake() with sdola as the recipient. critically, this step is preceded by redeeming 10.6m sdola in step 4, which burned those shares and collapsed totalsupply from 11.77m to just 1.16m. pre-attack, 87.9% of all sdola supply was deposited as collateral in the llamma — the attacker acquired and redeemed nearly all of it. with only 1.16m shares remaining, the 190k dola donation inflates converttoassets() by ~16%, rather than the ~1.6% it would have caused against the original 11.77m supply. this sequencing — drain supply first, then donate — is what made the oracle manipulation so cheap. oracle inflation alone also does not make any position liquidatable. when positions are not soft-liquidated, higher oracle = higher collateral value = better health. the oracle manipulation only becomes lethal after step 1 has placed all positions into soft-liquidation. combined effect when all steps execute in sequence, the result is devastating. the exchange (step 1) forces all positions into soft-liquidation and acquires 9.83m sdola for the attacker. the redeem (step 4) burns these shares, collapsing sdola supply from 11.77m to 1.16m. the donation (step 5) then inflates the oracle by ~16% (1.183 → 1.347) with just 190k dola — a fraction of what would be needed against the original supply. due to the cubic oracle sensitivity in the health formula (see section 5), this ~16% oracle increase translates to a ~35% reduction in x_down , pushing 27 of 30 soft-liquidated positions below zero health. only 3 positions with health above 27% survived. 5. why oracle up = health down this is counterintuitive: the oracle says collateral is worth more , yet positions become unhealthy . the explanation lies in the llamma health formula. health is computed as: health = get_x_down(user) / debt - 1 + liquidation_discount get_x_down() answers: "how much crvusd would this user's bands be worth if we adiabatically converted everything back?" it calls get_xy_up(user, false) in amm.vy l1286 . for bands where p_o > p_o_up (oracle is above the band — i.e., the band is fully soft-liquidated to crvusd), the conversion is: p_current_mid = p_o**2 // p_o_down * p_o // p_o_up # = p_o³ / (p_o_up * p_o_down) y_equiv = x * 10**18 // p_current_mid xy += y_equiv * p_o_up // sqrt_band_ratio which simplifies to: x down ​ = x ⋅ p o 3 ​ ⋅ band_ratio ​ p o , up 2 ​ ⋅ p o , down ​ ​ p_o is in the denominator, cubed. the ~13.8% oracle increase (1.183 → 1.347) translates to a ~35% decrease in x_down due to the cubic relationship, which drastically reduces health. for positions with only 1–5% health margin, this is instant death. the intuition: soft-liquidated bands hold crvusd. to value them, the amm asks "what would this crvusd buy if we converted back to sdola at current oracle?" higher oracle means sdola is more expensive, so the round-trip would yield less sdola back, producing a worse valuation. 6. impact category detail borrowers 27 of 30 positions hard-liquidated, ~$10.9m crvusd debt liquidated borrower losses ~$766k total (see section 6.1 for detailed breakdown) protocol no bad debt was generated. all liquidations completed fully — the protocol recovered debt from collateral. the attacker's undercollateralized re-borrow (step 7) was unwound within the same transaction sdola holders +14.3% windfall on converttoassets (190k dola permanently donated) attacker profit ~$245k net (6.74 weth + 227,326 dola − 0.024 eth gas) — see section 6.2 for funds flow 6.1 borrower losses how hard liquidation works in llamalend: when a position's health drops below zero, any third party can call controller.liquidate() . the liquidator repays the borrower's entire debt and in return seizes all collateral held in the borrower's llamma bands — both the remaining sdola and any crvusd from soft-liquidation. there is no separate "liquidation bonus" parameter; the liquidator's profit is simply the difference between the value of seized collateral and the debt repaid. this means the borrower's equity (collateral value − debt) is what the liquidator captures . although the market held ~$11.7m in notional collateral, this was not the amount at risk. the market's low loan discount (1.3%) allowed positions to operate at up to ~77x effective leverage, though actual leverage varied widely. most borrowers had borrowed close to their maximum, leaving only a thin equity buffer. methodology: for each of the 27 liquidated positions, we snapshot the pre-attack state (block 24,566,936) by reading each borrower's collateral (sdola + crvusd in bands) and debt from the controller. we convert collateral to crvusd-equivalent using the pre-attack oracle price (1.183). the borrower's loss is defined as: loss = collateral value (crvusd) − debt (crvusd) this represents the equity each borrower forfeited upon liquidation. the aggregate loss rate (total loss ÷ total collateral value) is 6.6%, reflecting the generally thin equity margins across positions. metric value positions liquidated 27 of 30 total collateral value ~$11.67m (crvusd equivalent) total debt repaid ~$10.9m crvusd total borrower loss (equity seized) ~$766k crvusd aggregate loss rate 6.6% of collateral value top 3 positions share of losses ~80% borrower losses in crvusd 6.2 funds flow the ~$766k in borrower equity seized through liquidations was the attacker's gross revenue. however, executing the attack required significant upfront costs, reducing net profit to ~$245k. attacker balance verification (pre/post attack): pre-attack post-attack delta attacker eoa eth 0.0969 0.0734 −0.0236 (gas) attacker eoa weth/dola/crvusd 0 / 0 / 0 0 / 0 / 0 — attack contract weth 0 6.7368 +6.7368 attack contract dola 0 227,325.57 +227,325.57 no other addresses received funds from the attack contract. the entire profit remained in the attack contract ( 0xd8e8544e0c808641b9b89dfb285b5655bd5b6982 ). flow amount direction borrower equity seized via liquidations ~$766k → attacker (gross revenue) attack execution costs (llamma swap losses, 190k dola donated via stake() , flash loan fees, gas, routing) ~$521k ← attack cost attacker net profit ~$245k 6.74 weth + 227,326 dola − 0.024 eth gas 7. root cause four factors combined to enable this attack: manipulable converttoassets() — dolasavings.stake(amount, recipient) is permissionless. anyone can stake dola on behalf of the sdola contract, inflating the share price without minting new shares. the sdola contract itself warns: "any protocol in which sudden, large and atomic increases in the value of an asset may be a security risk should not integrate this vault." no oracle smoothing on vault pps — the cryptofrompoolvaultwagg oracle applies an ema to the pool's price_oracle() but reads converttoassets() instantaneously. a single-block manipulation passes through directly. permissionless exchange() on llamma — anyone can dump arbitrary amounts of crvusd into the amm, force soft-liquidating all positions. under normal conditions this is economically irrational (bad swap rate), — the llamma's dynamic fee (introduced to mitigate oracle sandwich attacks) makes trading back to the oracle price unprofitable. however, the attacker bypassed this by using hard liquidation instead of trading back. the get_x_down() function used in health calculations does not account for dynamic fees when simulating what adiabatically trading to the oracle would do — so inflating the oracle makes positions appear unhealthy even though the dynamic fee would have prevented equivalent market trades. extreme supply concentration in llamma — 87.9% of all sdola supply was deposited as collateral in the llamma. this meant the attacker's single exchange() call simultaneously achieved two objectives: forcing all positions into soft-liquidation and acquiring nearly the entire sdola supply (9.83m of 11.77m). the attacker then redeemed this sdola, collapsing totalsupply from 11.77m to just 1.16m, which made the 190k dola stake() donation inflate pps by ~16% instead of ~1.6%. if the bulk of sdola supply had been held elsewhere (other dexes, wallets, protocols), the attacker would have needed separate transactions to accumulate enough shares before the attack — significantly increasing cost, complexity, and exposure to front-running. no single factor alone is sufficient. the attack requires all four. 8. cross-market risk assessment we have reviewed all other llamalend markets using vault-based oracles. the vulnerability exploited in this incident was specific to the sdola vault's permissionless stake() mechanism — other active vault collaterals (sfrax, sfrxusd, susds, yearn v3 vaults) use different accounting architectures that are not susceptible to this attack vector. no other markets are currently at risk. we are conducting further verification across all vault-collateral markets and working with the curve team on oracle-level mitigations to ensure this class of attack cannot be repeated against any future market. 9. recommendations oracle: apply ema/twap smoothing to converttoassets() reads in cryptofrompoolvaultwagg , matching the smoothing already applied to pool.price_oracle() add a per-block rate-of-change cap on vault pps readings collateral curation: establish a formal criterion for vault collateral onboarding: the vault's totalassets() must be resistant to atomic manipulation by unauthorized parties document the assessment methodology so it can be applied consistently to future vault collateral proposals

excerpt: LlamaRisk is engaged by the Curve DAO as an external risk-research and advisory services provider under the LlamaRisk Services Proposal — April 2026–2027 . The following is LlamaRisk's research view; it is not legal, tax, or inves
searchText: sdola repayment proposal — clarification on scope and liability operational state impaired markets llamarisk is engaged by the curve dao as an external risk-research and advisory services provider under the llamarisk services proposal — april 2026–2027 . the following is llamarisk's research view; it is not legal, tax, or investment advice. 1. llamarisk did not deploy, own, or operate the sdola-long2 market. llamalend markets are deployed and owned by parties holding the relevant on-chain authority. the original sdola market on llamalend was deployed by swiss stake, and the sdola-long2 instance was a subsequent redeployment carried out by another contributor with the same on-chain configuration when the issuer requested an updated arrangement. llamarisk neither held nor exercised the technical or governance authority required to deploy this market, and it does not now. 2. the oracle was set at deployment and is immutable. llamalend markets do not expose a mechanism to swap an oracle on a live market once deployed. this is a property of the market contracts themselves. the mitigation that curve has publicly described — a revised oracle framework — applies to future deployments and to llamalend v2, which is precisely consistent with the existing markets being immutable on this dimension. llamarisk could not have changed the oracle on this market, even if it had wished to and had not been asked to. 3. llamarisk's engagement does not extend to market deployment, oracle implementation, or smart contract code. the scope of llamarisk's services to the curve dao — set out in the publicly posted services proposal — is research, parameter analysis, monitoring, and advisory work. it does not include the deployment of markets, the authoring or selection of oracle contracts, or any smart contract development on which the affected market depended. liability for an outcome cannot, in our view, attach to a contributor for a function that the provider was neither retained to perform, authorised to perform, nor capable of performing. 4. llamarisk research is informational and disclaims liability for user losses. consistent with the disclaimers carried on llamarisk's published research and dashboards, llamarisk's outputs are provided for informational purposes and do not constitute investment, legal, tax, or financial advice. llamarisk does not custody user funds, does not direct user transactions, and does not assume liability for losses arising from third-party-deployed protocols or markets. 5. tabling a remediation proposal is not an admission of fault. the sdola-long2 repayment funds-source proposal identifies a possible dao-level funding source so that affected users can be made whole. it is a governance contribution to a community discussion about how the dao might respond — it does not allocate llamarisk capital, and it does not, on its face or by inference, accept responsibility on llamarisk's behalf.

searchText: [llamalend]: debt ceiling refinement operational state rollout llamalend v2 the op rollout is supported by an incentive campaign, so the initial borrow caps should avoid being so restrictive that they prevent organic market-rate discovery. the inital markets caps have been set with a conservative heuristic to identify the trade size at which slippage is equivalent to a liquidation discount. the caps should remain anchored to executable liquidation capacity under stress. method for fresh markets, borrower positions are not yet available, so liquidation pressure cannot be estimated from live vault-level data. instead, the cap is derived from stressed executable liquidity and a conservative borrower-behaviour assumption. the model first estimates how much collateral can be sold through available dex liquidity without making liquidation uneconomic. for each candidate route, the maximum executable collateral amount is identified subject to the liquidator’s usable price-impact margin: pi m a x ​ = θ − δ where θ is the liquidation discount and δ is an execution or price-duration loss buffer. route capacity is then stressed by a liquidity contraction factor λ liq ​ , and the model uses the deepest stressed route: x stress ​ = i max ​ λ liq ​ x i ∗ ​ ​ route capacities are not summed because aggregator routes may reuse overlapping underlying liquidity. since no live borrower distribution exists, the model uses a conservative sizing ltv. where reliable reference markets exist, the debt-weighted p95 borrower ltv can be used as the empirical behavioural assumption. if this empirical assumption does not produce a binding stress case, or if borrower behaviour is uncertain, the model falls back to the curve-derived max ltv: l m a x ​ = 1 − loan discount − 2 a n ​ the method then checks whether the stressed borrower ltv breaches a reduced-form hard-liquidation proxy: l hard ​ = 1 − θ the trigger shock required to reach this proxy is: s trigger ​ = 1 − l hard ​ l ​ where l is the chosen sizing ltv. the portion of the stress beyond this buffer is: ϕ = max ( 0 , s s − s trigger ​ ​ ) the term ϕ is not a probability; it is a stress-severity factor. if ϕ = 0 , the selected stress does not create hard-liquidation pressure under the assumed borrower behaviour, so the liquidity module is non-binding. llamma soft liquidation is incorporated through a soft-liquidation efficiency parameter η . residual hard-liquidation pressure is therefore scaled by: ( 1 − η ) ϕ the fresh-market cap is then: c fresh ​ = ( 1 − η ) ϕ x stress ​ ⋅ p s ​ ⋅ l ​ where p s ​ = p 0 ​ ( 1 − s ) is the shocked collateral price. this cap is binding only when the stress shock exceeds the borrower’s ltv buffer. once the market is live, this fresh-market approximation should be replaced with the live exposure-scale method using actual borrower positions and observed liquidation pressure. results wsteth–weth we refined the fresh-market borrow cap for the optimism wsteth/weth lending market under a 4.00% collateral price-shock scenario. the analysis uses current-price valuation, a 1.5% maximum liquidator price-impact tolerance, no assumed soft-liquidation efficiency, and a 1.5x liquidity contraction factor. a 1.5x contraction means usable liquidity is reduced to 66.7% of baseline, equivalent to a 33.3% reduction. soft-liquidation efficiency is set to 0% as a conservative assumption for this correlated-asset stress. the scenario represents a relative dislocation between wsteth and weth rather than a gradual broad-market move. because such basis shocks may occur quickly, or through liquidity/oracle dislocation, the analysis does not assume that llamma soft liquidation materially reduces residual hard-liquidation pressure before the stressed price level is reached. the executable liquidation route considered is wsteth → weth. baseline executable capacity is 256.88 wsteth, which falls to 171.25 wsteth after applying the liquidity contraction. the model computes max ltv from curve parameters at 95.52%. under the 4.00% price shock, stressed ltv rises to 99.50%, breaching the simplified hard-liquidation proxy of 98.5%. the implied trigger shock is approximately 3.02%, so the scenario exceeds the liquidation buffer. using the buffer-adjusted approach, the implied at-risk fraction is 24.49%. with soft-liquidation efficiency set to 0%, the residual buffer-adjusted hard-liquidation pressure is also 24.49% of exposure. this gives a buffer-adjusted borrow cap of approximately 824.18 weth-equivalent. recommended borrow cap: ~824 weth-equivalent. wbtc–usdc we refined the fresh-market borrow cap for the optimism wbtc/usdc lending market under a 9.40% collateral price-shock scenario. the analysis uses current-price valuation, a 5% maximum liquidator price-impact tolerance, 65% assumed soft-liquidation efficiency, and a 1.5x liquidity contraction factor. a 1.5x contraction means usable liquidity is reduced to 66.7% of baseline, equivalent to a 33.3% reduction. the executable liquidation route considered is wbtc → usdc. baseline executable capacity is 14.25 wbtc, which falls to 9.50 wbtc after applying the liquidity contraction. since only one route is used, there is no route aggregation or double-counting adjustment. the model computes max ltv from curve parameters at 89.92%. under the 9.40% price shock, stressed ltv rises to 99.24%, breaching the simplified hard-liquidation proxy of 95.0%. the implied trigger shock is approximately 5.35%, so the scenario exceeds the liquidation buffer. using the buffer-adjusted approach, the implied at-risk fraction is 43.07%. after applying 65% soft-liquidation efficiency, residual buffer-adjusted hard-liquidation pressure is 15.07% of exposure. this gives a buffer-adjusted borrow cap of approximately $4.38m. recommended borrow cap: ~$4.38m. wsteth–usdc we refined the fresh-market borrow cap for the optimism wsteth/usdc lending market under a 13.10% collateral price-shock scenario. the analysis uses current-price valuation, an 11% maximum liquidator price-impact tolerance, 65% assumed soft-liquidation efficiency, and a 1.5x liquidity contraction factor. a 1.5x contraction means usable liquidity is reduced to 66.7% of baseline, equivalent to a 33.3% reduction. the executable liquidation route considered is wsteth → usdc. baseline executable capacity is 339.01 wsteth, which falls to 226.01 wsteth after applying the liquidity contraction. since only one route is used, there is no route aggregation or double-counting adjustment. the model computes max ltv from curve parameters at 83.59%. under the 13.10% price shock, stressed ltv rises to 96.19%, breaching the simplified hard-liquidation proxy of 89.0%. the implied trigger shock is approximately 6.08%, so the scenario materially exceeds the liquidation buffer using the buffer-adjusted approach, the implied at-risk fraction is 53.60%. after applying 65% soft-liquidation efficiency, residual buffer-adjusted hard-liquidation pressure is 18.76% of exposure. this gives a buffer-adjusted borrow cap of approximately $2.66m. recommended borrow cap: ~$2.66m. conclusion once the op markets are live, these fresh-market assumptions should be replaced by the live exposure-scale method using actual borrower positions and observed liquidation pressure. to summarise, we recommend conservative starting caps market previous cap refined cap change comment wbtc–usdc $1.5m usdc ~$4.38m ~2.9x increase refined cap uses the buffer-adjusted fresh-market method, wbtc → usdc executable liquidity, 65% soft-liquidation efficiency, and max-ltv fallback because the empirical 80% ltv case was non-binding. wsteth–usdc $400k usdc ~$2.66m ~6.7x increase refined cap uses the buffer-adjusted fresh-market method, wsteth → usdc executable liquidity, 65% soft-liquidation efficiency, and max-ltv fallback. wsteth–weth 126 weth (~$0.3m) ~824 weth-equivalent ~6.5x increase refined cap uses the buffer-adjusted fresh-market method, wsteth → weth executable liquidity, max-ltv/high-ltv assumption, and 0% soft-liquidation efficiency to reflect sudden correlated-asset basis dislocation risk. appendix borrower ltv behaviour in reference markets to further refine the pre-launch cap assumptions, we reviewed reference curve lend v1 markets on ethereum and measured observed borrower ltv behaviour: ltv = collateral_up × oracle price debt ​ for each proxy market, we compared historical ltvs, latest per-user ltvs, and debt-weighted ltvs. debt-weighted ltv is the most relevant metric for borrow-cap sizing because caps are constrained by debt demand, not by the number of users. unweighted ltv can overemphasize small accounts, while p99 can be noisy and sensitive to outliers or liquidation-adjacent positions. the preferred behavioural input is therefore the historical debt-weighted p95 ltv, with the latest debt-weighted p95 used as a sanity check. this captures aggressive but still representative borrower behaviour and avoids assuming that every borrower sits exactly at the maximum allowed ltv. results wbtc–usdc → proxied by wbtc-crvusd llamalend v1 market wsteth-usdc → proxied by wsteth-crvusd llamalend v1 market wsteth-weth → proxied by sreusd-crvusd and sfrxeth-crvusd looping markets llamalend v1 market sreusd-crvusd sfrxusd-crvusd proposed assumption for further refinement deployment proxy market debt-weighted p95 suggested assumption wbtc–usdc wbtc-crvusd ~79.7% historical; ~69.6% latest 80% base case wsteth–usd wsteth-crvusd ~79.4% historical; ~75.0% latest 80% base case wsteth–weth looping proxy set sfrxusd-crvusd ~96.8–97.0%; sreusd-crvusd ~92.3–95.3% max-ltv / high-ltv assumption for new markets, this empirical assumption can be used as the base case. if the empirical-ltv scenario does not breach the hard-liquidation buffer under the stress scenario, the liquidity constraint is considered non-binding under that behavioural assumption. we tested this for some market this holds true. in that case, we additionally run a max-ltv fallback to produce an actionable initial cap.

title: [LlamaLend]: Reserve Factor Scan
sourcePath: Handover Package/Operational State/Rollout LlamaLend V2/[LlamaLend]: Reserve Factor Scan.html
excerpt: This analysis benchmarks possible LlamaLend V2 protocol take-rates against comparable lending and vault systems. The core question is how much borrower interest or vault yield can be retained by the protocol, DAO, vault manager, o
searchText: [llamalend]: reserve factor scan operational state rollout llamalend v2 this analysis benchmarks possible llamalend v2 protocol take-rates against comparable lending and vault systems. the core question is how much borrower interest or vault yield can be retained by the protocol, dao, vault manager, or curator before the remainder is passed to suppliers. two measures are used. gross take-rate measures the total supplier yield haircut. protocol-only take-rate estimates the portion that accrues specifically to the protocol or dao where identifiable. method the benchmark combines aave v3, euler v2, and morpho vault v2 data from dune. the data points are not 100% comparable due to mechanical differences in protocol. aave and euler are closest because both measure a share of borrower interest diverted before suppliers receive yield. morpho vault v2 is less directly comparable because it measures a vault performance fee on native yield, not necessarily a borrower-side reserve factor or protocol revenue. for aave, we look at the reserve factor. reserve factor is the “percentage of interest accrued by borrowers that is allocated to the aave treasury” ( aave, n.d. ) . the dune query uses newreservefactor the reserve-factor change events. this is treated as both gross and protocol-only take-rate because the reserve factor captures the share of borrower interest allocated to protocol reserves. for euler v2, the benchmark uses the evault interestfee as the gross_take_rate . euler states that when interest accrues, a portion is allocated to fees, controlled by the vault governor as interestfee ; fees dilute depositors by the interestfee fraction of interest. euler’s protocolconfig then determines the fee share between the vault governor and euler dao. therefore, protocol_only_take_rate it is estimated as interestfee × protocol_fee_share . this is close to aave conceptually, but not identical, because euler can split the fee between dao and vault governor. ( euler, n.d. ) for morpho vault v2, the query uses vault performance fees as gross take-rate. these are included in the gross distribution but excluded from the protocol-only take-rate because the fee recipient is not necessarily morpho protocol revenue. for morpho vault v2, the benchmark uses newperformancefee from morpho_v2_multichain.vaultv2_evt_setperformancefee . morpho defines the performance fee as a cut on the native yield earned by allocating capital, capped at 50%. this is comparable as a gross yield take-rate, but it is not necessarily protocol revenue, because the recipient can be a curator or vault-level fee recipient. therefore, protocol_only_take_rate is omitted and not available for morpho. ( morpho, n.d. ) overall, aave and euler are the most comparable because both are borrower-interest fees. morpho vault v2 is useful as a benchmark for what vault depositors tolerate as a yield haircut, but it should be labelled separately as a vault-yield fee. results source: dune the gross take-rate distribution is heavily concentrated around 0%, 5%, 10%, and 15 to 20%. the largest visible cluster is around 10%, driven by both euler and morpho vault v2 observations. aave contributes more heavily to the higher-rate region, especially around 15 to 20%, 45%, and 50%, with a few extreme values near 95%. this suggests that 10–20% is the common benchmark range, while values above 25–30% exist but are more aggressive and mostly market-specific. source : dune the protocol-only take-rate distribution is narrower because morpho vault v2 is excluded. euler shows a strong concentration around 5%, reflecting cases where the gross interest fee is split between euler dao and the vault governor. aave protocol-only take-rates are more dispersed, with visible clusters around 10% to 20% and 45% to 50%. this means aave provides evidence that high protocol-level take-rates exist, but they should not be interpreted as a universal default. conclusion we recommend a default rate of 10% take-rate. fee’s split to incentivize crvusd usage could be handled separately with a fee splitter contract. as a soft target, we recommend 5%, with the other 5% being shared with the asset issuer. the optimal take-rate should be market-specific, not fixed globally. it depends on how sensitive borrowers are to higher rates and how sensitive suppliers are to reduced yield. competitive blue-chip markets likely need lower fees to remain attractive, while more specialized, riskier, or highly curated markets may support higher fees.

searchText: [llamalend]: sdola migration note operational state rollout llamalend v2 llamalend v2 — mainnet market selection & initial market parameters sdola / crvusd migration note sdola and dola have already operated in a live llamalend setting, and the relevant risk question is not whether the collateral category is new to curve, but whether the specific failure mode identified in the sdola-long2 incident has been removed in the migrated configuration. apart from the march 2026 oracle/pps manipulation incident, the market’s core issue was not persistent malfunction of the collateral asset or normal market operation, but a legacy oracle design in which the vault pps leg was read instantaneously while the pool oracle leg was smoothed. the migration report, therefore, focuses on a hard market configuration rather than duplicating a full collateral due-diligence report. 5. llamalend-specific parameters 5.1 oracle design the planned oracle construction is proposed as follows: p sdola/crvusd ​ = p dola/crvusd ng ​ × pps sd o l a / d o l a ​ where: p sdola/crvusd ​ = final oracle price. p dola/crvusd ng ​ = stableswapng state price derived from the sdola/scrvusd pool, read in the correct orientation. pps sdola/dola ​ = current erc4626 price-per-share of sdola , obtained through converttoassets . the sdola/crvusd oracle can be derived from the sdola/scrvusd stableswapng pool ( 0x76a962ba6770068bcf454d34dde17175611e6637 ) because both pool assets are configured as erc4626 tokens ( asset_type = 3 ). under this configuration, the pool’s internal rate logic calls converttoassets for each vault token before computing the amm state price. as a result, the pool price is computed on normalized underlying balances: dola for sdola and crvusd for scrvusd , rather than on raw vault-share balances. the final oracle therefore combines the pool-implied dola/crvusd state price with the current sdola price-per-share. the implementation should explicitly verify the pool coin order and invert the pool price if the oracle is read in the opposite orientation. 5.2 market parameters market parameters are copied mechanically from the previous market. the relevant parameters are: parameter value a 285 fee 0.002 loan_discount 0.01 liquidation_discount 0.013 5.3 exposure limits the sdola/crvusd borrow-cap estimate was produced using the fresh-market sizing mode. since this is treated as a fresh market, the method does not rely on observed borrower positions. instead, it converts stressed executable liquidation capacity into a borrow-cap estimate using an assumed borrower ltv, a price-shock scenario, and a residual hard-liquidation pressure model. the empirical price shock was estimated from the sdola/crvusd 1-minute ohlc feed. the liquidity-capacity input, however, was based on the dola → crvusd route. this is intentional: sdola represents a claim on underlying dola, and liquidated sdola can be unwrapped into dola before execution. since dola/crvusd liquidity is deeper than direct sdola/crvusd liquidity, the executable liquidation-capacity estimate uses the underlying dola route, subject to the assumption that unwrapping remains available and does not introduce material additional delay or loss during the stress window. route capacities are not summed, because different routes may share the same underlying liquidity. at a maximum accepted liquidation slippage of 1.0%, the observed dola → crvusd route capacity was 3.83m dola. this was divided by a 1.5× liquidity-contraction factor, giving a stressed executable capacity of 2.55m dola. the market parameters imply a maximum ltv of: l m a x ​ = 1 − loan discount − 2 a n ​ using a loan discount of 1.3%, (a = 285), and (n = 4), this gives: l m a x ​ = 97.998 the hard-liquidation ltv proxy is: l hard ​ = 1 − liquidation discount = 99.0 the borrower ltv assumption was set equal to maximum ltv. this is conservative but appropriate for this use case, because these markets are expected to be primarily used for looping strategies, where borrowers are likely to operate close to the maximum allowed ltv. the empirical shock input was estimated using a 60-minute downside window-shock method on the sdola/crvusd price feed. the shock extraction used downside direction, a top-50 event selection, a 60-minute declustering window, a 1.5× trigger multiplier, and selected the mean of the top declustered downside events. this produced an empirical price shock of: s empirical ​ = 0.4172 this empirical shock is not a simple rolling es estimate. it is an event-based downside stress estimate designed to avoid overweighting many overlapping observations from the same price episode. the declustering step is important because rolling 60-minute returns from 1-minute data are highly overlapping; without declustering, a single depeg episode can generate many near-duplicate observations and distort the tail estimate. however, the empirical shock alone is below the model-implied hard-liquidation trigger: s trigger ​ = 1 − l hard ​ l m a x ​ ​ = 1.0119 since the empirical shock of 0.4172% does not breach this threshold, it does not create hard-liquidation pressure under the buffer model. to avoid falling back to a full-pressure assumption while still producing a binding cap-sizing scenario, the structural-trigger policy was used. this sets the sizing shock equal to the trigger shock plus a 25 bps margin: s sizing ​ = s trigger ​ + 0.25 = 1.2619 this produces a shocked price of 0.9839 and a stressed ltv of 99.25%. under this scenario, the model estimates that 19.81% of the assumed borrower exposure becomes residual hard-liquidation pressure. soft-liquidation efficiency was set to 0%. this means the model does not credit soft liquidation with reducing hard-liquidation pressure over the short stress horizon. this is intentionally conservative: for a short 60-minute stress window, the analysis assumes that soft-liquidation execution may not reliably absorb the adverse move before hard-liquidation pressure has to be cleared through external dola/crvusd liquidity. the resulting buffer-adjusted borrow cap is: 12.43 m the full-pressure cap is also reported as a conservative lower-bound diagnostic: 2.46 m this result should be interpreted as a conservative structural-trigger cap for sdola/crvusd using dola/crvusd executable liquidity after unwrapping. the empirical shock was non-binding; the final sizing scenario intentionally uses the model-implied liquidation trigger plus margin to ensure that the cap reflects a realistic buffer-breach stress without defaulting to the overly conservative full-pressure assumption. parameter value borrow cap 12,400,000 crvusd warning: cap estimates are dynamic and should be monitored closely and actively managed. 5.4 monetary policy source: secondarymp tool parameter value alpha 0.5 beta 5 target_utilization 90% rate_shift 0 sdola is yield-bearing, so an ema-following secondary monetary policy may be appropriate if the yield anchor is robust, observable, and manipulation-resistant. however, the migration should avoid creating persistent recursive carry where users can borrow crvusd, acquire dola/sdola, and loop the position at excessive leverage. recommendation the sdola/crvusd market can be considered for migration without a full new collateral assessment, provided the migrated configuration directly addresses the legacy oracle failure mode. the key gating item is oracle safety: the new market should only proceed if the sdola pps leg is protected against atomic manipulation and if the oracle can be updated or replaced through the llamalend v2 oracle architecture. market parameters and the initial borrow cap should be refreshed conservatively, with post-migration monitoring of borrower concentration, route liquidity, and oracle behavior.

searchText: [llamalend]: sfrxusd/crvusd operational state rollout llamalend v2 llamalend v2 — mainnet market selection & initial market parameters sfrxusd and frxusd should be treated as a migration-style onboarding rather than a fully new collateral category. the relevant risk question is not whether the asset type is unfamiliar, but whether the migrated market configuration correctly handles the wrapper structure, oracle path, and liquidation execution route. sfrxusd is a yield-bearing erc4626 wrapper over frxusd, while frxusd itself is the more liquid underlying asset. for this reason, the market configuration should price the wrapper through its price-per-share, but size executable liquidation capacity through the deeper frxusd/crvusd route after unwrapping. the migration report therefore focuses on hard market configuration: oracle construction, parameter selection, route-liquidity sizing, and borrow-cap calibration. a full collateral due-diligence report is not duplicated here, provided the migrated market explicitly relies on the underlying frxusd liquidity path and the sfrxusd price-per-share leg is implemented in a manipulation-resistant way. 5. llamalend-specific parameters 5.1 oracle design the planned oracle construction is proposed as follows: p sfrxusd/crvusd ​ = pps sfrxusd/frxusd ​ × p frxusd/crvusd ​ where: p sfrxusd/crvusd ​ = final oracle price. pps sfrxusd/frxusd ​ = erc4626 price-per-share of sfrxusd , expressed in underlying frxusd . p frxusd/crvusd ​ = frxusd/crvusd pegkeeper stableswapng ( 0x13e12bb0e6a2f1a3d6901a59a9d585e89a6243e1 ). the oracle should price sfrxusd as a claim on underlying frxusd. the wrapper leg contributes the current sfrxusd price-per-share, while the market leg converts the underlying frxusd value into crvusd terms. 5.2 market parameters market parameters are aligned with the migrated stable-wrapper configuration. the relevant parameters are: parameter value a 285 fee 0.002 loan_discount 0.013 liquidation_discount 0.01 the resulting maximum ltv is: l m a x ​ = 1 − loan discount − 2 a n ​ using a loan discount of 1.3%, a = 285 , and n = 4 , this gives: l m a x ​ = 97.998 this corresponds to approximately 50.0× gross looping leverage: max leverage = 1 − l m a x ​ 1 ​ ≈ 50.0 × 5.3 exposure limits the sfrxusd/crvusd borrow-cap estimate was produced using the fresh-market sizing mode. since this is treated as a fresh market, the method does not rely on observed borrower positions. instead, it converts stressed executable liquidation capacity into a borrow-cap estimate using an assumed borrower ltv, a price-shock scenario, and a residual hard-liquidation pressure model. the empirical price shock was estimated from the frxusd/usd 1-minute chainlink feed and converted into the relevant frxusd/crvusd pricing context. the liquidity-capacity input, however, was based on the frxusd → crvusd route. this is intentional: sfrxusd represents a claim on underlying frxusd, and liquidated sfrxusd can be unwrapped into frxusd before execution. since frxusd/crvusd liquidity is deeper than direct sfrxusd/crvusd liquidity, the executable liquidation-capacity estimate uses the underlying frxusd route, subject to the assumption that unwrapping remains available and does not introduce material additional delay or loss during the stress window. route capacities are not summed, because different routes may share the same underlying liquidity. at a maximum accepted liquidation slippage of 1.0%, the observed frxusd → crvusd route capacity was 8.71m frxusd. this was divided by a 1.5× liquidity-contraction factor, giving a stressed executable capacity of 5.81m frxusd. the initial frxusd/crvusd price was set from the observed token reference prices: p frxusd/crvusd ​ = p crvusd/usd ​ p frxusd/usd ​ ​ = 0.9986373659 0.9995843452 ​ = 1.0009482715 the hard-liquidation ltv proxy is: l hard ​ = 1 − liquidation discount = 99.0 the borrower ltv assumption was set equal to maximum ltv. this is conservative but appropriate for this use case, because these markets are expected to be primarily used for looping strategies, where borrowers are likely to operate close to the maximum allowed ltv. the empirical shock input was estimated using a 60-minute downside window-shock method on the frxusd/usd price feed. the shock extraction used downside direction, a top-50 event selection, a 60-minute declustering window, a 1.5× trigger multiplier, and selected the mean of the top declustered downside events. this produced an empirical price shock of: s empirical ​ = 0.0810 the top-event distribution was mild: the top-50 median shock was 0.0398%, the mean was 0.0810%, the p90 was 0.1059%, and the maximum selected event was 0.9361%. this empirical shock is not a simple rolling es estimate. it is an event-based downside stress estimate designed to avoid overweighting many overlapping observations from the same price episode. the declustering step is important because rolling 60-minute returns from 1-minute data are highly overlapping; without declustering, a single depeg episode can generate many near-duplicate observations and distort the tail estimate. however, the empirical shock alone is below the model-implied hard-liquidation trigger: s trigger ​ = 1 − l hard ​ l m a x ​ ​ = 1.0119 since the empirical shock of 0.0810% does not breach this threshold, it does not create hard-liquidation pressure under the buffer model. to avoid falling back to a full-pressure assumption while still producing a binding cap-sizing scenario, the structural-trigger policy was used. this sets the sizing shock equal to the trigger shock plus a 25 bps margin: s sizing ​ = s trigger ​ + 0.25 this produces a shocked price of 0.9883 and a stressed ltv of 99.25%. under this scenario, the model estimates that 19.81% of the assumed borrower exposure becomes residual hard-liquidation pressure. soft-liquidation efficiency was set to 0%. this means the model does not credit soft liquidation with reducing hard-liquidation pressure over the short stress horizon. this is intentionally conservative: for a short 60-minute stress window, the analysis assumes that soft-liquidation execution may not reliably absorb the adverse move before hard-liquidation pressure has to be cleared through external frxusd/crvusd liquidity. the resulting buffer-adjusted borrow cap is: 28.40 m the full-pressure cap is also reported as a conservative lower-bound diagnostic: 5.63 m the full-pressure cap represents the conservative bound obtained by assuming that the full residual borrower exposure must be liquidated through external liquidity, without applying the ltv-buffer adjustment that reduces pressure when only a fraction of positions breaches the hard-liquidation threshold. this result should be interpreted as a structural-trigger buffer-adjusted cap for sfrxusd/crvusd using frxusd/crvusd executable liquidity after unwrapping. the empirical shock was non-binding; the final sizing scenario intentionally uses the model-implied liquidation trigger plus margin to ensure that the cap reflects a realistic buffer-breach stress without defaulting to the overly conservative full-pressure assumption. the gap between the buffer-adjusted cap and the full-pressure cap is driven by the fact that, under the structural-trigger scenario, only 19.81% of assumed borrower exposure is modeled as residual hard-liquidation pressure. parameter value borrow cap 28,400,000 crvusd warning: cap estimates are dynamic and should be monitored closely and actively managed. 5.4 monetary policy sfrxusd is yield-bearing, so an ema-following secondary monetary policy may be appropriate if the yield anchor is robust, observable, and manipulation-resistant. however, the migration should avoid creating persistent recursive carry where users can borrow crvusd, acquire frxusd/sfrxusd, and loop the position at excessive leverage. source: secondarymp tool parameter value alpha 0.5 beta 5 target_utilization 90% rate_shift 0 recommendation the sfrxusd/crvusd market can be considered for migration without a full new collateral assessment, provided the migrated configuration explicitly addresses the wrapper and liquidation-path risks. market parameters and the initial borrow cap should be refreshed conservatively, with post-migration monitoring of borrower concentration, route liquidity, unwrap availability, and oracle behavior.
