searchText: [llamalend]: susdf collateral onboarding assessment operational state rollout llamalend v2 llamalend v2 — mainnet market selection & initial market parameters executive summary this report evaluates susdf as proposed collateral for an ethereum mainnet curve llamalend market with crvusd as the borrow asset. falcon describes susdf as the yield-bearing version of usdf, minted when usdf is deposited into falcon’s erc-4626 vaults, with value accruing through the susdf-to-usdf exchange rate. the collateral risk chain is therefore: susdf → usdf → falcon reserve / redemption / governance / custody / strategy stack susdf inherits the core usdf risks: reserve quality, redemption access, kyc dependence, issuer discretion, off-chain strategy execution, custody, and governance. it also adds wrapper-specific risks: erc-4626 accounting, pps correctness, vault upgradeability, reward-distribution mechanics, and liquidity of the staked wrapper. 1. asset fundamental characteristics 1.1 asset susdf is the yield-bearing wrapper for usdf, falcon finance’s overcollateralized synthetic dollar. usdf can be minted by users who have completed falcon’s onboarding requirements and have deposited approved collateral. for approved stablecoin collateral, usdf is minted through the classic mint process at a 1:1 ratio. for approved non-stablecoin collateral, users may use either the classic mint or the “innovative mint” process, both of which rely on overcollateralization so that the value of deposited collateral exceeds the value of minted usdf. the underlying usdf asset is not backed by a single collateral type. falcon accepts stablecoins, non-stablecoin cryptoassets, and real-world-asset exposures such as tokenized gold, tokenized stocks, tokenized u.s. treasuries, and tokenized corporate credit. falcon’s collateral framework screens eligible assets based on exchange listing quality, liquidity, open interest, funding-rate stability, and broader market conditions. this makes usdf a synthetic dollar backed by a diversified collateral and strategy stack rather than a narrow fiat-reserve stablecoin. after minting, collateral is routed through falcon’s custody and trading infrastructure. falcon uses third-party custodians and off-exchange settlement infrastructure to support centralized-exchange activity while reducing direct exchange-custody exposure. falcon then deploys collateral into yield-generating strategies. the relevant strategy set includes positive and negative funding-rate arbitrage, collateral or native asset staking, cross-exchange arbitrage, spot/perpetuals arbitrage, statistical arbitrage, options-based strategies, and liquidity provision. susdf sits one layer above this usdf system. falcon describes susdf as the yield-bearing version of usdf, minted when usdf is deposited into falcon’s erc-4626 vault. the amount of susdf received depends on the prevailing susdf-to-usdf exchange rate. as falcon generates yield, newly minted usdf is allocated into the susdf vault, increasing the amount of usdf redeemable per unit of susdf over time. 1.2 architecture falcon’s architecture has two layers relevant to this market. the first is the usdf minting and reserve-management layer. the second is the susdf vault layer, where usdf is deposited to receive a yield-bearing erc-4626 share token. usdf minting users who have passed kyc requirements are allowed to mint usdf by depositing approved collateral assets. users are allowed to mint usdf through two methods: classic mint or innovative mint. suppose a user chooses to mint using an approved stablecoin; the classic mint method is used, where usdf is returned at a 1:1 ratio. if a user chooses to mint using an approved non-stablecoin asset, either the classic or innovative mint method can be used. in both methods, usdf is not returned at a 1:1 ratio. for innovative mint, the user selects a lockup period, strike price, and capital efficiency level, which determines the amount of usdf eligible to be minted. for classic mint, the user simply deposits an accepted asset and receives usdf. these methods always utilize an overcollateralization ratio, making sure that the backing collateral is always greater in value than the minted usdf. users can also acquire usdf from secondary marketplaces. this diagram illustrates the minting flow of usdf tokens, showing interactions between off-chain and on-chain components. off-chain, the user submits an order via the falcon ui, which is validated, hashed, and signed by the minter/custodian. the signed order is sent on-chain to the precollateralizedminter contract via precollateralizedmint() , which then calls the usdf token contract’s mint() function to issue tokens to the user. current accepted collateral falcon’s currently listed supported collateral set includes stablecoins, non-stablecoin cryptoassets, and tokenized real-world assets. these assets are accepted subject to falcon’s collateral acceptance framework , which screens assets for binance listing, spot/perpetual availability, cross-exchange or dex liquidity, funding-rate stability, open interest, market depth, and overall risk grade. category currently listed supported assets stablecoins usdt, usdc, dai, usds, usd1, fdusd major / non-stablecoin cryptoassets btc, wbtc, eth, sol, xrp, trx, ton, pol, wlfi, eos, near, dexe, beamx, move, fet, coti, avax, qi, sei, dolo, mnt, trump, enzobtc real-world assets xaut, tslax, crclx, nvdax, mstrx, spyx, ustb reserve architecture falcon routes deposited collateral into third-party custodians and off-exchange settlement infrastructure. according to falcon finance’s transparency page , ceffu and fireblocks are key custody providers, yet with the majority of reserves (~95%) being held in their own multisig wallet. susdf vault architecture susdf is created when usdf is deposited into falcon’s erc-4626 vault. users receive susdf according to the prevailing susdf-to-usdf exchange rate. falcon calculates generated yield daily, mints new usdf from that yield, and deposits a portion of the newly minted usdf into the susdf vault. this increases the amount of usdf redeemable per unit of susdf over time. flowchart td a[user holds usdf] --> b[deposit usdf into susdf erc-4626 vault] b --> c[susdf minted to user] c --> d[user holds transferable yield-bearing susdf] e[falcon strategies generate yield] --> f[yield calculated daily] f --> g[new usdf minted from generated yield] g --> h[portion deposited into susdf vault] h --> i[susdf : usdf exchange rate increases] d --> j{user exit route} j -->|unstake / redeem vault share| k[receive usdf based on current pps] j -->|sell on secondary market| l[exit through susdf liquidity] k --> m[usdf can be held, traded, or redeemed through falcon] yield source source: faclon documentation redemptions falcon distinguishes between susdf unstaking and usdf redemption. susdf can be unstaked into usdf immediately, whereas usdf redemption into underlying collateral is subject to a 7-day cooldown. falcon also documents a brief daily lock window around yield calculation, during which staking and unstaking interactions may be queued. peg stability mechanism usdf’s peg mechanism relies on three linked stabilizers: active hedging, overcollateralization, and arbitrage. falcon states that collateral deposited to mint usdf is managed through delta-neutral and market-neutral strategies to reduce directional exposure to the underlying collateral assets. in parallel, usdf minted against non-stablecoin collateral is overcollateralized, so the collateral value is intended to exceed the value of usdf issued. the market peg is then supported by arbitrage: when usdf trades above $1, kyc-approved users can mint usdf and sell it externally; when usdf trades below $1, users can buy discounted usdf and redeem it for collateral value through falcon. for susdf, this peg mechanism matters indirectly: susdf accrues value in usdf terms, but its final collateral value still depends on usdf remaining close to its intended dollar value. 1.3 tokenomics susdf tokenomics are primarily defined by its vault-share mechanics. users deposit usdf into falcon’s susdf erc-4626 vault and receive susdf based on the prevailing susdf-to-usdf exchange rate. susdf is therefore not designed to remain fixed at 1.00 usdf. instead, its value should increase relative to usdf as yield is allocated to the vault. yield accrues through the susdf-to-usdf exchange rate. falcon calculates generated yield daily across its strategies, mints new usdf from that yield, and deposits a portion of the newly minted usdf into the susdf vault. this increases the amount of usdf redeemable per unit of susdf. the source of susdf yield results from trading strategies (see 1.2. architecture under yield source) and depends on their success. 2. market risk 2.1 liquidity to estimate current on-chain liquidity depth, we aggregated swap quotes from kyberswap, paraswap, and odos for susdf and usdf → crvusd trades ranging from 1 to 10 million (s)usdf. we then fitted an isotonic regression to the aggregated data, allowing us to identify the most favorable executable quotes across aggregators for each trade size. susdf: the chart suggests that slippage increases materially once sell orders exceed approximately 1 million susdf against crvusd, indicating limited depth at larger trade sizes. usdf since susdf can be atomically redeemed for usdf, we also examine the underlying liquidity profile of usdf to assess the effective liquidation capacity available to market participants. 2.2 volatility as usdf is the primary driver of susdf volatility. we calculate daily log returns from hourly price data and aggregate them into a daily volatility metric. source : dune 2.3 exchanges source : dex screener current market data suggests that liquidity exists primarily at the usdf layer, not the susdf layer. the attached dex screenshot shows several ethereum usdf pools, with the largest visible venues being a usdf/usdt uniswap v3 pool with approximately $10.0m liquidity, a usdf/usdc curve pool with approximately $3.3m liquidity, and a usdf/usdt pancakeswap v3 pool with approximately $1.0m liquidity. source: coingecko the attached cex screenshot shows usdf trading primarily on mexc and bitfinex. the strongest visible centralized usdf market is mexc usdf/usdt, with approximately $466k 24h volume and around $109k / $114k of ±2% order-book depth. mexc also lists usdf pairs against usdc, btc, eth, and ff, but the visible ±2% depth on non-stablecoin pairs is materially smaller. bitfinex markets appear much thinner in the screenshot, with limited 24h volume and asymmetric depth. centralized liquidity may support overall price formation, but permissionless llamalend liquidations should be sized primarily against executable on-chain routes. 2.4 growth susdf supply peaked toward the end of september and has since been in steady decline, which aligns with the broader crypto market cycle. source: dune the circulating supply of usdf shows a similar picture, with a contraction of close to 1 billion usdf from the market peak to the current point. source: dune yet on a relative basis, usdfs market share has stayed approximately the same despite the contraction. this suggests that changes might be largely due to the overall sentiment cooling in crypto markets, rather than disinterest in usdf and susdf among cryptoassets. source: dune note: we excluded busd, usdc, usdt, dai, and fpi for visual clarity. usdf is depicted in neon. 2.5 peg of usdf usdf peg quality has been decreasing over recent months, as visible from the chart below, where usdf gradually trades below the 1 dollar peg. source: dune looking at absolute deviation makes this picture clearer - with a sustained increase. source: dune 3. technological risk 3.1 smart contract risk falcon’s official docs list the susdf contract and the susdf staking rewards distributor on ethereum mainnet. falcon also states that usdf and susdf were audited by zellic and pashov , with no critical or high-severity vulnerabilities identified in either assessment. falcon’s github repository is not public, yet deployed contracts and documentation are available. usdf is natively deployed on ethereum , which has logic implemented via a transparentupgradeableproxy proxy pattern. usdf is also natively deployed on binance smart chain, but has no proxy implementation. users can bridge between ethereum and binance smart chain using a third-party application or chainlink's ccip. finally, usdf can also be bridged to xrpl via axelar . usdf can be staked into susdf on ethereum, which has logic implemented via a transparentupgradeableproxy proxy pattern. the susdf staking rewards distributor can be viewed here and does not have a proxy implementation. the contract for restaked usdf positions represented as erc-721 nfts can be viewed here and has a proxy implementation. 3.2 bug bounty program llamarisk’s earlier usdf review stated that falcon planned to launch a bug bounty program within q1 2026. however, as of this review, no public bug bounty or formal vulnerability-disclosure program covering usdf, susdf, the staking rewards distributor, or related oracle contracts could be independently verified. 3.3 dependency risk falcon uses collateral from usdf to generate yield in several ways, all of which bring some third-party risk. on-chain liquidity strategies involve liquidity pools that rely on third-party protocols. this makes falcon vulnerable to exploit of a partner protocol, which could result in a loss of funds. falcon currently uses well-established on-chain liquidity pools. this includes uniswap, curve, and pancakeswap on ethereum and binance smart chain. the liquidity pools are paired against core stable assets such as usdt, usdc, usd1, as well as smaller pools with frxusd. the liquidity pools that falcon uses introduce potential dependencies, as these liquidity pools are reliant on these on-chain protocols. native altcoin staking also brings in dependency risk. falcon states that they use professional staking service providers, such as luganodes, when staking altcoins. altcoins are only staked if there is a negotiated zero lock-up period, allowing falcon to swiftly exit positions in times of market volatility. falcon relies on two custodial solutions to house funds and utilize off-exchange settlement. although these custodians bring third-party risk, the risk is minimized through diversification and multisig/mpc measures. minting functions for usdf occur entirely off-chain. falcon states that they use an internal price oracle that integrates over 40 trading venues to calculate an internal fair price. this reduces the dependency risk by utilizing a diverse selection of data sources; however, the off-chain oracle process is not publicly available. the integration of chainlink ccip bridging has a strong security record, but also brings additional risks as a third-party application. 4. counterparty risk 4.1 governance and regulatory risk susdf inherits the regulatory, reserve-management, and issuer-discretion risks of usdf because it is ultimately a yield-bearing claim on usdf. falcon digital limited is the issuer-facing entity identified in falcon’s terms, which are governed by british virgin islands law. falcon states that it is not currently licensed by any regulatory authority. the usdf report further notes that falcon obtained a bvi-law memorandum concluding, subject to its assumptions, that usdf is not an “investment” under siba and that falcon, acting solely as issuer, would not require vasp registration. this conclusion remains dependent on the actual scope and location of falcon’s activities, particularly where custody, transfer, minting, redemption, or issuer-related financial services are carried on from the bvi. usdf reserve safeguards are primarily contractual and operational rather than imposed by a prudential regime. falcon maintains voluntary overcollateralization for usdf minted against non-stable collateral, with asset-specific buffers adjusted for volatility, liquidity, and slippage. it also operates an on-chain insurance fund and publishes reserve information through a transparency dashboard and regular ht digital collateral letters. however, the published collateral letters are point-in-time reports and explicitly do not verify ownership, control, or whether assets are encumbered. reserve protection therefore depends on falcon’s internal risk controls, custody arrangements, and ability to maintain clean title and liquidity across its reserve portfolio. the reserve and redemption structure is permissioned. minting and redemption require kyc/kyb, redemption is subject to a minimum size and a seven-day processing period, and falcon retains broad discretion to apply restrictions, suspend accounts, monitor activity, or block transactions. falcon’s terms also restrict u.s. persons and users in sanctioned or otherwise restricted jurisdictions. the usdf implementation includes an on-chain restriction mechanism that can prevent transfers involving addresses placed on a denylist. these controls may support sanctions compliance and incident response, but they mean issuer redemption is not an immediate, permissionless liquidation backstop. the main regulatory and governance risk for susdf is therefore not only the legal status of the token itself, but the continued functioning of the underlying falcon issuer, reserve-management, custody, compliance, and redemption framework. this risk is amplified by the heterogeneous nature of usdf reserve assets, which may include stablecoins, cryptoassets, and tokenized real-world assets with different custody, transferability, and regulatory characteristics. for llamalend, liquidation assumptions should rely on secondary-market liquidity rather than guaranteed issuer redemption, while ongoing monitoring should cover reserve disclosures, custody concentration, changes in access restrictions, and material changes to falcon’s legal or regulatory status. 4.2 access control risk the default_admin_role for the usdf proxy contract is set to a 4/6 multisig . this role has the ability to pause/unpause transfers and manage a blacklist, allowing for swift responses to security threats. the signers are: 0x804016c31e52805eb00e0ef42126fd3e980a0b33 - identified as falcon contract deployer 0xf4161ed9cfa2ac91068556387f9ce225fce6893f 0xe313dbd8693d656fe760ba3e766c80eb08f06734 0xa91472acc85272fd4119a946796aaf6c8392b0c0 0x276c580545293da6c7c0fdd12038cc75accbd211 0xa76095b4a145055c3cc46ed64dd1bcf8a8544e6c the contract is giving mint rights to precollateralizedmint, which has a minter role set to the following address: 0x57dd832f0d9547fca3aa3cceb052c2fd8818bf4d . operational security practices falcon finance maintains a policy of discretion regarding specific operational security protocols to maximize protection. the protocol employs a hybrid operational model, with a dedicated core team that ensures agile and decisive management. falcon has launched a governance framework to empower community participants to vote on protocol developments. falcon enforces a robust management practice where at least 3 members of the trading team must work on each strategy, reducing the risk of a single member making an exploitable mistake. there are currently no timelocks implemented in core falcon finance contracts, meaning that administrative actions have no enforced delay. 5. llamalend-specific parameters 5.1 oracle design the planned oracle construction is proposed as follows: p susdf/crvusd ​ = p crvusd/usdc ​ pps susdf/usdf ​ × p usdf/usdc ​ ​ where: p susdf/crvusd ​ = final oracle price pps susdf/usdf ​ = erc-4626 price per share vault ( 0xc8cf6d7991f15525488b2a83df53468d682ba4b0 ) p usdf/usdc ​ = stableswapng pool of usdf/usdc ( 0x72310daaed61321b02b08a547150c07522c6a976 ) p crvusd/usdc ​ = pegkeeper stableswap ng usdc/crvusd ( 0x4dece678ceceb27446b35c672dc7d61f30bad69e ) concern: where the pool used in the collateral oracle is also a material liquidation venue, limited liquidity can create a self-reinforcing liquidation loop. a usdf sell-off lowers the pool price; positions then approach or cross liquidation thresholds, causing additional usdf collateral to be sold through the same pool or routing path. those sales further deepen the imbalance and depress the oracle-relevant price, potentially triggering further liquidations before arbitrage capital can restore the peg. the risk is therefore not only insufficient exit capacity at a fixed price, but endogenous deterioration of the liquidation trigger itself as liquidation flow feeds back into the oracle market. the severity depends on the oracle hard-liquidation pressure under the buffer model. to avoid falling back to a full-pressure assumption while still producing a binding cap-sizing scenario, the structural-trigger policy was used. this sets the sizing shock equal to the trigger shock plus a 25 bps margin: s sizing ​ = s trigger ​ + 0.25 this produces a shocked price of 0.9744 and a stressed ltv of 98.85%. under this scenario, the model estimates that 12.05% of the assumed borrower exposure becomes residual hard-liquidation pressure. soft-liquidation efficiency was set to 0%. this means the model does not credit soft liquidation with reducing hard-liquidation pressure over the short stress horizon. this is intentionally conservative: for a short 60-minute stress window, the analysis assumes that soft-liquidation execution may not reliably absorb the adverse move before hard-liquidation pressure has to be cleared through external usdf/crvusd liquidity. the resulting structural-trigger buffer-adjusted borrow cap is: 3.86 m the full-pressure cap is also reported as a conservative lower-bound diagnostic: 0.465 m the full-pressure cap represents the conservative bound obtained by assuming that the full residual borrower exposure must be liquidated through external liquidity, without applying the ltv-buffer adjustment that reduces pressure when only a fraction of positions breaches the hard-liquidation threshold. this result should be interpreted as a structural-trigger buffer-adjusted cap, not as a full-pressure liquidation cap. the empirical shock was non-binding; the final sizing scenario intentionally uses the model-implied liquidation trigger plus margin to ensure that the cap reflects a buffer-breach stress without defaulting to the overly conservative full-pressure assumption. the gap between the buffer-adjusted cap and the full-pressure cap is driven by the fact that, under the structural-trigger scenario, only 12.05% of assumed borrower exposure is modeled as residual hard-liquidation pressure. summary parameter value borrow cap 3,800,000 crvusd warning: cap estimates are dynamic and should be monitored closely and actively managed. 5.4 monetary policy susdf is yield-bearing, so we recommend adapting an ema-following secondary monetary policy. the susdf yield at the time of parameterisation was 5.1%. source: secondarymp tool parameter value alpha 0.5 beta 5 target_utilization 90% shift 0 rate calculator rate source: linear vesting, the stakedusde pattern. rewards arrive through transferinrewards , set vestingamount , and vest over vestingperiod (24h). we checked on-chain that totalassets = usdf.balanceof(susdf) - getunvestedamount() . while the window is open: rate = vestingamount * 1e18 / vestingperiod / totalassets # 0 after the window ends contract address susdf vault 0xc8cf6d7991f15525488b2a83df53468d682ba4b0 usdf 0xfa2b947eec368f42195f24f36d2af29f7c24cec2 the one thing the calculator has to get right is window-gating: it must return 0 once block.timestamp passes lastdistributiontimestamp + vestingperiod , otherwise it keeps reporting yield during a gap when nothing is actually vesting and the ema holds that stale number instead of decaying. a large transferinrewards does spike the in-window rate, but that needs no special handling, the same ema and 150% cap that bound syrupusdc bound it here too. this is an instantaneous rate, not an average, so it tracks real yield while falcon tops up rewards on its usual daily cadence and the ema turns the sawtooth into a usable base rate. if rewards stop, the gate sends the rate to 0 and the ema settles on the 1% floor. recommendation we recommend not listing, or, if really desired, a very cautious listing of susdf, with conservative risk parameters and a low borrow cap. our key concerns include: deteriorating usdf peg quality , with a sustained increase in deviations from the intended $1 peg over recent months. limited liquidation capacity , where liquidity is relatively shallow for usdf and susdf oracle-liquidation feedback risk , as the proposed oracle relies on a liquidity venue that may also serve as a primary liquidation route, potentially amplifying market stress during adverse conditions. centralized redemption and governance dependencies , including kyc-gated redemptions, issuer discretion, custody concentration, and upgradeable contracts without timelock protections. complex reserve composition , where usdf value ultimately depends on a heterogeneous mix of crypto assets, tokenized rwas, custodial arrangements, and active yield-generation strategies. disclaimer this review was independently prepared by llamarisk, a community-led decentralized defi risk organization. llamarisk is not directly affiliated with the protocol(s) reviewed in this assessment and did not receive any compensation from the protocol(s) or their affiliated entities for this work. the information provided should not be construed as legal, financial, tax, or professional advice.

searchText: [llamalend]: syrupusdc collateral onboarding assessment operational state rollout llamalend v2 llamalend v2 — mainnet market selection & initial market parameters executive summary syrupusdc is a yield-bearing stablecoin (erc-4626) backed by maple direct's overcollateralized institutional loan book. this assessment evaluates its suitability as collateral for llamalend across asset fundamentals, market liquidity, technological, and counterparty risk. the material difference for llamalend is the oracle-to-liquidation path. unlike hard-threshold lending markets, llamalend liquidates continuously through llamma, which requires the collateral to be sold into on-chain liquidity as the oracle price falls. syrupusdc's value is a function of an off-chain loan book whose impairments are marked discretely on-chain. this creates a specific, real risk surface — the marking-lag window and thin secondary exit liquidity — that does not exist for simple liquid collateral. we document this in a dedicated section below (section 4a) and treat it as the binding consideration for parameterization. the single largest driver of potential value loss is loan-book concentration: the largest single loan in the syrupusdc pool is $200m (~15.5% of the pool's ~$1.29b open-term book), the most concentrated borrower holds ~$262m (~20.4%), and the top three borrowers hold ~49% of pool principal; three borrowers also operate across both maple pools, together ~29% of combined principal (all api-verified, june 17, 2026). a default on the largest loan would mark syrupusdc's nav down in a single block. this is the basis for the ltv methodology to be developed separately: the market's maximum ltv must sit below the value that survives a single-largest-loan default, otherwise an impairment instantly produces bad debt for crvusd lenders. 1. asset fundamental characteristics 1.1 asset syrupusdc is a tokenized note over a loan book backed by collateralized liquid digital assets. it is best characterized as a concentrated yield-bearing stablecoin; structurally it is an underlying and segregated pool of usdc issued to independent, kyc'd institutional borrowers underwritten by maple direct. the syrupusdc erc-4626 vault represents the sum of all usdc deposited into the pool. a portion of backing is held as readily available redemption liquidity, deployed across defi venues; the remainder is lent out as open term loans. yield is therefore derived from both active loans and defi yield on the liquidity buffer. the current maple direct model is overcollateralized, crypto-asset-backed lending — not unsecured commercial credit (the latter describes maple's earlier, deprecated 2021–22 model). permissioned institutional borrowers (trading firms, market makers, funds) draw usdc and pledge liquid crypto collateral (btc, eth, xrp, etc.) worth more than the loan, maintained above 100% collateralization at all times. borrowers complete kyc/aml and underwriting that assesses balance-sheet strength and the operational ability to meet margin calls quickly in falling markets. collateral is held in institutional custody (e.g. anchorage, bitgo, zodia), with on-chain custody addresses published for verification. critically, the usdc disbursement and loan accounting are on-chain (the loan-manager contracts), while collateral custody, margin-call cure, and liquidation are executed off-chain / otc — the on-chain/off-chain split that underlies the marking-lag risk in section 4a. a portion of pool assets is held as recallable, multi-chain redemption liquidity (ethereum, bnb, solana, base, arbitrum, plasma, mantle). over the trailing three months, maple's annualized returns declined to ~4–5%, down from the 6–9% range observed in mid-2025. the pool's gross open-term loan book stands at ~$1.29b across 40 active loans with zero impaired (api-verified, june 17, 2026); this gross figure includes treasury/amm and basis-trade allocations alongside secured credit. collateral composition is disclosed off-chain by maple and is not on-chain/api-verifiable: it has historically been btc-dominated (~75% of secured collateral) with xrp the next sleeve, and collateralization ratios vary by asset (volatile collateral such as hype held at higher ratios, ~1.76x; stablecoin/treasury near 1.00x). see appendix a for the live breakdown. relevance to llamalend : syrupusdc's redemption value is the loan book's value. the composition above — concentrated, btc-dominated, off-chain-collateralized — is what determines how much value syrupusdc can lose in a default, and is carried forward into the maple-default risk surface (section 4a) and the ltv methodology. 1.1.1 asset composition and yield sources syrupusdc's backing is not exclusively secured credit. pool assets ( totalassets ≈ $1.305b on-chain at the time of writing) consist of the gross open-term book (~$1.29b, api-verified) plus a small residual cash buffer. critically, the supporting strategies below are themselves booked inside that gross open-term figure rather than as a separate buffer, so the gross number is not all secured credit. per maple's disclosures, the declared scope is: overcollateralized institutional lending (primary). syrupusdc blends two secured sleeves: blue chip secured — btc/eth collateral, lower yield, tight collateral ratios (~1.0–1.1x). high yield secured — more volatile collateral (xrp, hype, sol, …), higher yield, higher required collateral ratios (e.g. hype at 1.76x). futures basis trading — cash-and-carry capturing btc futures term-structure spreads. defi liquidity provision — idle usdc deployed into defi protocols (aave, fluid, etc.) to support the instant-redemption buffer. t-bills — short-dated treasury exposure. this means a portion of syrupusdc's value depends on strategies beyond the secured loan book; the loan book is roughly half of total pool assets, the remainder being buffer/treasury operations. the full live book is detailed in appendix a . declared collateral and loan criteria. collateral is evaluated for liquidity, historical volatility, and technical security; assets without acceptable liquidity are ineligible. concentration limits are applied so maple is never too large a share of any single market (to bound liquidation slippage), more volatile collateral requires higher collateral-to-loan ratios, and liquidation levels are set conservatively above 100% collateralization. each loan carries its own initial / margin-call / liquidation levels; a breach of the margin-call level triggers a 24-hour cure window before otc liquidation under the borrower's legal agreement. maple reports zero losses to date. these are operational policies and track record, not protocol-enforced guarantees — the distinction the ltv methodology must price. relevance to llamalend : syrupusdc's redemption value is the loan book's value. the composition above — concentrated, btc-dominated, off-chain-collateralized — is what determines how much value syrupusdc can lose in a default, and is carried forward into the maple-default risk surface (section 4a) and the ltv methodology. 1.2 architecture fixed-rate loan underwriting and liquidity management are operated on ethereum by maple. the token is an immutable erc-20 / erc-4626 vault; redemptions are processed through a withdrawal queue. redemption performance has improved over time and is relevant to liquidation viability (see section 2.1 and section 4a): withdrawal-queue median time-to-process: 3.6 minutes ; size-weighted average 1.21h. 91.4% of redemptions (90.9% of volume) settle within the hour. tail risk concentrates in 320 events exceeding 24 hours (~65.4m usdc), worst case 124.7h. these are typically smaller, older requests rather than recent large ones. weekly size-weighted averages show only 9 weeks ever crossed the 24-hour threshold, all in the early operating period; recent weeks are near zero, indicating the pool is now sized to absorb redemptions as they arrive. relevance to llamalend : primary redemption (mint/redeem at nav) is one of the two exit paths a liquidator/arbitrageur has when unwinding soft-liquidated syrupusdc. fast redemption helps in normal conditions; however, redemption is at the current nav and is subject to the available liquidity buffer — both of which degrade precisely in the default scenario that matters (section 4a). 1.3 tokenomics syrupusdc total supply has no fixed cap; it expands and contracts with usdc deposits and redemptions. supply peaked at ~1.66b on march 22, 2026 and stood at ~1.06b at the time of writing. following the kelp exploit (april 18, 2026), elevated cross-market rates prompted significant withdrawals, contracting circulating supply on ethereum. despite this, defi utilization of syrupusdc remained elevated. 1.3.1 token holder concentration top holders of syrupusdc (ethereum, at the time of writing): sky amlproxy : 49.6% chainlink ccip tokenpool : 17.1% spark: liquidity layer : 8.5% morpho : 7% eoa 1 : 2% the top 5 control ~84.2% of supply, predominantly held by defi applications (top-5 eoas only ~4.8%). concentration in protocol/defi hands is broadly positive for liquidity stability but means a small number of integrations drive most secondary-market flow. 2. market risk 2.1 liquidity swap liquidity for syrupusdc within a 7.5% price impact stands at 12.35m (~$14.35m) , up from ~10.28m ($11.41m) over recent months. simulated routes indicate most swaps within this range are facilitated via uniswap and fluid pools, so syrupusdc has deep primary liquidity to cover liquidations in normal conditions . 2.1.1 liquidity venue concentration ethereum mainnet liquidity is predominantly in the uniswap v4 syrupusdc/usdc pool , with additional depth on fluid. 2.1.2 dex lp concentration a maple-controlled wallet remains the majority liquidity provider, supplying ~$15m in usdc on uniswap v4 via arrakis. secondary liquidity is therefore reliant on a single venue and a single, protocol-aligned source . relevance to llamalend : this is the most important market-risk caveat for an llamma market. soft-liquidation depends on arbitrageurs buying syrupusdc out of the amm and offloading it on-chain. the bulk of executable exit liquidity is maple-provided and concentrated in one pool; under a maple-default scenario this same liquidity can widen or be withdrawn (see section 4a, t3). stressed executable liquidity — not headline $14.35m spot depth — is the correct benchmark for liquidation-discount and exposure sizing. 2.2 volatility the syrupusdc/usdc conversion rate on uniswap v4 tracks the internal exchange rate closely, trading at a mean discount of ~9 bps . the largest absolute secondary-market deviation observed was 22 bps (april 20, 2026, during the kelp exploit event), which mean-reverted. there has been no sustained (≥2% for ≥2 days) deviation from the internal rate. 2.3 exchanges syrupusdc is exclusively traded on dexs and is not currently listed on any centralized exchange. there is no cex exit path for liquidators. 2.4 growth supply has contracted from its march 2026 peak but defi utilization remains high. growth is demand-driven (no emissions-based incentives sustaining the peg); the asset trades on its yield and redemption guarantees rather than mercenary liquidity. 3. technological risk 3.1 smart contract risk maple's contracts carry an extensive audit history. six additional audits were completed across recent contract upgrades: governor timelock upgrade : sherlock (sept 2025) — 3 low/informational; 0xmacro (sept 2025) — 1 low, addressed. withdrawal manager upgrade : spearbit (nov 2025) — 1 high (fixed) + 4 informational; sherlock (nov 2025) — none. ccip receiver release : dedaub (nov 2025) — none; sigma prime (jan 2026) — 6 low + 7 informational, closed/resolved. 3.2 bug bounty program the immunefi bounty with a maximum payout of $500k remains active. 3.3 price feed risk the pricing path is the central technological consideration for the llamalend market. proposed oracle construction. the market prices the collateral (syrupusdc) against the debt asset (crvusd) as the product of two legs: p(syrupusdc / crvusd) = converttoexitassets(syrupusdc → usdc) × ema( usdc/crvusd pool price ) leg 1 — price-per-share, converttoexitassets . this converts one syrupusdc into its usdc redemption value. the correct read is converttoexitassets (not converttoassets ): only converttoexitassets reflects unrealizedlosses , i.e. it steps down immediately when a loan is impaired, whereas converttoassets ignores impairment and would keep printing full nav. reading the exit rate is what allows the oracle to recognize a marked impairment in the same block. this leg is not smoothed — smoothing it would delay recognition of a downward mark, which is exactly the move the market must react to. leg 2 — usdc/crvusd pool price with ema. this converts the usdc value into crvusd terms using the on-chain usdc/crvusd curve pool price, ema-smoothed. smoothing this leg dampens transient pool noise and manipulation of the usdc/crvusd quote without blunting the impairment signal, which lives in leg 1. pricing usdc against crvusd via the live pool (rather than assuming 1 usdc = 1 crvusd) means a usdc depeg relative to crvusd is captured directly by the oracle. note that maple internally hardcodes usdc to $1 inside its usdoracle (referenced from the maple global contract ). this is internal to maple's own loan-book accounting and is distinct from the llamalend oracle above; since usdc is maple's loan asset, the static $1 assumption only affects maple's nav on an upward usdc depeg (debt undervalued), historically rare and short-lived given active arbitrage — low in practice. key oracle limitation (carried into section 4a). leg 1 only moves when maple marks an impairment on-chain. it is blind to off-chain credit deterioration and to dex repricing in the interval between a loan going bad and the delegate calling impairloan() . the exchange rate can be rate-limited on the upside (to resist redemption-rate manipulation) but cannot anticipate a downside mark, and — per above — leg 1 is deliberately left unsmoothed so the mark is recognized promptly. the remaining tunable is the ema window on leg 2 and llamma's own texp / limit_p_o , which are section 5 calibration decisions. manipulation resistance on the pps leg. because converttoexitassets is a vault price-per-share read, it is structurally exposed to the single-block pps-inflation class of attack seen in the sdola-long2 incident, where a permissionless donation to the underlying vault was used to atomically spike the oracle and force liquidations. that vector is dormant for syrupusdc today — its ~1.1b supply is externally held and cannot be cornered, redemptions are queued rather than atomic, and donating against a ~$1.3b asset base to move pps by any meaningful amount is prohibitively expensive — but the protection is purely economic and could erode if supply contracted or a single market came to hold a large share of it. we therefore convert this into a structural guarantee with two complementary controls on the pps leg: (1) an upward rate-limit / cap on converttoexitassets , so the oracle cannot accept an instantaneous jump in share price regardless of cause; and (2) a very short ema over the read. even a short window makes single-block manipulation infeasible — a one-block donation contributes only ≈ δt/texp of weight (on the order of a percent or two), so an attacker would have to sustain the donation across many blocks, which de-atomizes the attack, removes flash-loan financing, and exposes the donated capital to arbitrage. the window is kept deliberately short so that downside recognition of a genuine maple impairment is delayed only by minutes — negligible against the hours-scale, discretionary marking lag at t0 (section 4a) that dominates syrupusdc's actual risk. 3.4 dependency risk loan collateral syrupusdc's effective collateral set is concentrated around bitcoin and assets native to secondary networks — xrp ledger and hyperliquid . these operate on chains with distinct security assumptions and network-specific market dynamics, and their liquidation is conducted off-chain/otc by maple. this concentration is the dependency that propagates into syrupusdc's redemption value during a default (section 4a). infrastructure the mainnet market's primary external dependency is maple's own loan-management and impairment machinery. (the base instance additionally depends on chainlink ccip; out of scope for this mainnet assessment.) 4. counterparty risk 4.1 governance and regulatory risk syrupusdc is issued by maple direct, which operates a kyc/aml-gated institutional lending business. the primary regulatory considerations are the centralized, permissioned nature of borrower onboarding and the off-chain legal enforceability of the loan agreements that back the token. these are inherent to the credit model rather than specific to any single venue, and are reflected in the counterparty and maple-default risk surfaces below. 4.2 access control risk controlling multisigs on mainnet: dao multisig: 4/7 operational admin: 3/5 safe security admin: 3/6 the manager variable controls core operational logic (redemption processing, max mints/withdrawals) and is set to the maplepoolmanager , controlled by the governor timelock. the governor timelock implements role-based access control: role controlling addresses role_admin dao multisig (4/7), eoa 1 (identified as mpc) executor_role operational admin (3/5 safe), eoa 2 proposer_role dao multisig (4/7) canceller_role security admin (3/6) 4.2.2 timelock duration delays exposed by the governor timelock : default min delay: 3 days; default execution window: 2 days min_delay: 1 day; min_execution_window: 1 day custom function-specific delays can be set via setfunctiontimelockparameters . relevance to llamalend : the impairment/default path that drives nav is operated by these privileged roles (impairment requires investment committee sign-off + 3-of-5 multisig). nav adjustments are therefore discretionary in timing — the protocol cannot assume impairments are marked promptly. this discretion is the source of the marking-lag risk in section 4a. 4a. the maple-default risk surface (llamalend-specific) this is the risk that most distinguishes a syrupusdc llamalend market from one collateralized by a simple liquid asset, and the one that should govern parameterization. syrupusdc's value is a function of an off-chain loan book whose losses are recognized on-chain only when maple marks them. in a continuous-liquidation system like llamma, the interaction between discrete nav marks and thin secondary exit liquidity defines the bad-debt risk. why a default loses value at all the loans are originated off-chain but are collateralized (btc, xrp, eth, custodied). when a borrower defaults, maple liquidates that collateral otc and applies proceeds to principal. the loss to the pool = principal − recovery from the collateral sale. that loss is booked as unrealizedlosses / realizedlosses , and syrupusdc nav drops by loss / totalassets in a single block: converttoexitassets = (totalassets − unrealizedlosses) / totalsupply recovery is not automatically 100%: the largest loan carries a permissive 95.2% liquidation level , btc can gap through that level in a thin otc window, and concentration means a correlated move can impair several loans at once. the size of this loss is the subject of the ltv methodology (to be developed separately). concentration — the magnitude driver observed loan-book composition: largest single loan: $200m (~15.5% of the pool's ~$1.29b book) — btc-collateralized at a permissive 95.2% liquidation level per maple's off-chain disclosures, a wide margin-call-to-liquidation band relative to peers. most concentrated borrower: ~$262m (~20.4% of the pool) across two loans; the top three borrowers hold ~49% of pool principal (api-verified). the two maple pools are not independent risk silos : three borrowers operate across both pools and together hold ~$486m (~29% of combined principal) ; the largest cross-pool borrower holds ~$235m ($60m in syrupusdc + $175m in syrupusdt, ~13.9% of combined) — cross-pool overlap verified via borrower addresses in the api. a single default hits syrupusdc and syrupusdt lenders concurrently. margin calls have historically been cured within hours (observed instances include a $200m and a $30m loan both cured within 48h via off-chain collateral top-ups), but cure is an off-chain, discretionary process — not a protocol guarantee. liquidation processing (off-chain → on-chain) maple's procedure is: monitor → margin call (12–24h cure window) → otc liquidation → and only then reflect any shortfall on-chain. impairment requires investment committee sign-off + 3-of-5 multisig and books the residual as unrealizedlosses ; the terminal default step books realizedlosses and permanently lowers the exchange rate. a legal default alone does not automatically move the on-chain rate — the on-chain mark is a discretionary, multi-step action. timeline of a default through llamma t0 — loan goes bad, before maple acts. on-chain state unchanged: issuancerate still running, unrealizedlosses still 0, converttoexitassets still prints full nav. off-chain reality is already impaired — informed traders see the missed payment and begin dumping syrupusdc on uniswap; dex price drops below nav. the oracle is blind to this. this marking-lag window — where nav does not match the real redemption price — is the single most dangerous moment, because llamma will not begin soft-liquidating a position that the oracle still believes is healthy. t1 — delegate calls impairloan() (discretionary timing). the loan's issuancerate is pulled, principal + accrued interest is booked into unrealizedlosses , and nav drops in the same block by the impaired fraction. this is exactly why the oracle must read converttoexitassets (which captures unrealizedlosses ) and not converttoassets (which would not move). t2 — llamma digests the drop. the oracle price p_o falls x% in one block. llamma's limit_p_o caps how fast its internal price can track the external oracle per block, spreading the move over several blocks rather than gapping instantly. this is amm self-protection against oracle manipulation; it incidentally cushions the discontinuity. soft-liquidation begins as p_o falls. t3 — liquidation execution (the real test). soft-liquidation must find buyers. arbitrageurs buy syrupusdc out of the amm only if they can offload it downstream, and post-default they have two degraded options: (1) redeem at maple — now queued/congested, at the new lower nav, against a finite (~$0.6m instant) buffer; or (2) sell on uniswap — a ~$15m, single-source pool, already trading below nav. arbitrageurs will not fill at the oracle's nav; they wait for the amm price to drop further to clear the market discount. soft-liquidation becomes sluggish or partial , positions linger in syrupusdc, and if the drop exceeds the borrower's ltv buffer the position goes underwater → bad debt to crvusd lenders. parametrization because an impairment marks nav down in one block and exit liquidity is thin and concentrated, the market's maximum ltv must sit below the value that survives a single-largest-loan default . if max ltv exceeds that, the impairment instantly produces bad debt rather than a soft-liquidatable position. quantifying that ceiling — the loss-given-default of the largest loan as a fraction of nav, plus an execution buffer, with maple default probability sizing the buffer — is the subject of the ltv methodology to be developed in a follow-up. 5. llamalend v2 specific parameters 5. llamalend-specific parameters 5.1 oracle design the planned oracle construction is proposed as follows: p syrupusdc/crvusd ​ = p crvusd/usdc ​ pps syrupusdc/usdc ​ ​ where: p syrupusdc/crvusd ​ = final oracle price pps syrupusdc/usdc ​ = erc-4626 price per share vault ( 0x80ac24aa929eaf5013f6436cda2a7ba190f5cc0b ) p crvusd/usdc ​ = pegkeeper stableswap ng usdc/crvusd ( 0x4dece678ceceb27446b35c672dc7d61f30bad69e ) 5.2 market parameters we parameterise market parameter ( a , fee , loan_discount , and liquidation_discount ) using the llammasimulator. as input feed, we constructed a dune-sourced pps of syrupusdc and paired it with a dune-sourced crvusd/usd feed . syrupusdc was launched as an asset on may 21, 2024. however, the retrieved data only covers the period from october 15, 2024, to june 15, 2026. given that this asset is 3.5% 5.3 exposure limits the syrupusdc/crvusd is treated as a fresh market, the method does not rely on observed borrower positions. instead, it converts stressed executable liquidation capacity into a borrow-cap estimate using an assumed borrower ltv, a price-shock scenario, and a residual hard-liquidation pressure model. the liquidity-capacity input is based on the syrupusdc → crvusd route. route capacities are not summed, because different routes may share the same underlying liquidity. at a maximum accepted liquidation slippage of 0.6%, the observed route capacity was 8.28m syrupusdc. this was divided by a 1.5× liquidity-contraction factor, giving a stressed executable capacity of 5.52m syrupusdc. the market parameters imply a maximum ltv of: l m a x ​ = 1 − loan discount − 2 a n ​ using a loan discount of 1.8%, (a = 312), and (n = 4), this gives: l m a x ​ = 97.559 the hard-liquidation ltv proxy is: l hard ​ = 1 − liquidation discount = 99.4 the borrower ltv assumption was set equal to maximum ltv. this is conservative but appropriate for this use case, because these markets are expected to be primarily used for looping strategies, where borrowers are likely to operate close to the maximum allowed ltv. the empirical shock input was estimated from the syrupusdc/crvusd price feed using a 60-minute downside window-shock method. the shock extraction used downside direction, a top-50 event selection, a 60-minute declustering window, a 1.5× trigger multiplier, and selected the mean of the top declustered downside events. this produced an empirical price shock of: s empirical ​ = 0.2007 the top-event distribution was relatively mild: the top-50 median shock was 0.1316%, the mean was 0.2007%, the p90 was 0.3123%, and the maximum selected event was 1.0544%. this empirical shock is not a simple rolling es estimate. it is an event-based downside stress estimate designed to avoid overweighting many overlapping observations from the same price episode. the declustering step is important because rolling 60-minute returns from 1-minute data are highly overlapping; without declustering, a single depeg episode can generate many near-duplicate observations and distort the tail estimate. however, the empirical shock alone is below the model-implied hard-liquidation trigger: s trigger ​ = 1 − l hard ​ l m a x ​ ​ = 1.8521 since the empirical shock of 0.2007% does not breach this threshold, it does not create hard-liquidation pressure under the buffer model. to avoid falling back to a full-pressure assumption while still producing a binding cap-sizing scenario, the structural-trigger policy was used. this sets the sizing shock equal to the trigger shock plus a 25 bps margin: s sizing ​ = s trigger ​ + 0.25 this produces a shocked price of 1.1456 and a stressed ltv of 99.65%. under this scenario, the model estimates that 11.89% of the assumed borrower exposure becomes residual hard-liquidation pressure. soft-liquidation efficiency was set to 0%. this means the model does not credit soft liquidation with reducing hard-liquidation pressure over the short stress horizon. this is intentionally conservative: for a short 60-minute larger haircut despite a higher liquidation level. it is also cross-pool, so its default hits syrupusdc and syrupusdt together. exposure size alone hides this; the loss-after-recovery ranking surfaces it. size ≠ risk. the largest borrower by exposure ($242m pyusd/ustb treasury) contributes near-zero loss (~$4m stressed), confirming that ranking by principal would mis-identify the binding scenario. ltv implication taking the stressed scenario as the working stress ( l nav ​ ≈ 2.5%) gives a ceiling of ~97.5% before b exec ​ ; the severe scenario (~4.1%) gives ~95.9%. applying a b exec ​ of 3–5% for thin, single-source syrupusdc exit liquidity lands a defensible max ltv in the ~91–94% range, to be finalized with the llammasimulator and the chosen confidence level. note that the llamma effective ltv is delivered through loan_discount and band count n , so this ceiling is the input to those parameters in section 5, not a directly-set threshold. b.8 limitation: collateral correlation (single-borrower vs systemic stress) this methodology measures the single most damaging borrower default in isolation. that is the right binding constraint for setting an ltv floor, but it understates tail risk, because the loan book's collateral is highly correlated: btc, cbbtc, eth and xrp all sell off together in a broad crypto crash. in such an event: most high-ltv / thin-cushion loans would breach their liquidation levels at roughly the same time , so realized loss would be the aggregate across many loans — not one $200m borrower. otc and on-chain exit liquidity is shared and finite ; when every position liquidates at once, executable haircuts rise above the per-asset figures in b.4 (the haircut should itself become a function of aggregate liquidation volume, not a fixed per-collateral constant). the cross-pool overlap (~29% of combined principal, appendix a) means syrupusdc and syrupusdt liquidate into the same stressed venues simultaneously. this correlation title: [LlammaLend]: How much worse are Chainlink Oracles really?
sourcePath: Handover Package/Research/Chainlink vs Curve Oracles/[LlammaLend]: How much worse are Chainlink Oracles really.html
excerpt: Introduction On-chain price feeds derived from liquidity pools are inherently vulnerable to manipulation, particularly under conditions of low liquidity or targeted trading. Oracle networks such as Chainlink mitigate this risk by
searchText: [llammalend]: how much worse are chainlink oracles really? research chainlink vs curve oracles introduction on-chain price feeds derived from liquidity pools are inherently vulnerable to manipulation, particularly under conditions of low liquidity or targeted trading. oracle networks such as chainlink mitigate this risk by aggregating prices across venues, providing a more robust reference. however, llamma-based soft-liquidation mechanisms rely on smooth price evolution, while chainlink updates occur discretely within predefined deviation thresholds. this creates a potential tension between robustness and smoothness. the objective of this report is to evaluate this trade-off for btc pricing, comparing oracle-based and pool-based feeds within a controlled simulation framework. llammasimulator: chainlink vs. binance method we evaluate btc price feeds using a llamma simulation framework, benchmarking against binance btc–usdt as a proxy for price discovery. alternative feeds include chainlink btc–usd on ethereum and op, as well as the wbtc–usdt price from the curve finance tricrypto pool. all feeds are aligned to a common time window to ensure comparability. market parameters are calibrated on the binance feed and then held fixed across all runs, isolating the effect of the oracle. performance is evaluated across the loss distribution using three sampling regimes: extreme tail outcomes (500,000 simulations, top 50), adverse scenarios (100,000 simulations, top 10,000), and full-distribution averages (50,000 simulations). to isolate the role of price smoothness, additional smoothing is disabled (ema = 1), ensuring that observed differences arise from the intrinsic structure of each feed. for the smoothing feed, we only look at the adverse scenarios. results feeds chainlink and curve feeds appear smoother than binance in variance terms, but this is driven by sparse updates rather than continuous pricing. both exhibit very high zero-return rates (80–97% vs ~4% for binance), implying stepwise price paths with discrete jumps rather than smooth evolution. as a result, they are statistically smoother but pathwise less continuous, which is the dimension most relevant for llamma performance. for the curve pool, we used the prices ohlc endpoint, yet it is unclear to what extent this reflects the on-chain path. comparison of feeds the comparison reflects differences between centralized exchange pricing and two distinct on-chain pricing mechanisms: chainlink btc/usd feeds (on ethereum and op) and a dex-derived price from curve finance (tricrypto pool). both chainlink feeds track binance closely, with spreads centered near zero. the curve feed—derived from the curve’s tricrypto pool—shows substantially wider spreads, heavy tails, and time-varying variance. lagged correlation results show peak alignment at zero lag across all feeds, indicating no persistent lead–lag structure relative to binance. however, correlation strength differs markedly: op feed is highest, eth feed moderate, and curve lowest. the op feed shows tighter dispersion and higher correlation than ethereum, indicating slightly stronger alignment, likely due to differences in update latency or network conditions. the curve-based price deviates materially, with wider spreads, heavy tails, and weaker correlation. this reflects its dependence on amm liquidity and pool imbalances rather than external price aggregation. comparison of simulation results performance tail-loss performance results tail-loss results (500k sims, top 50) show clear separation across feeds. relative to binance, the chainlink eth feed slightly improves tails (~−3% mean), with limited dispersion. the op feed worsens tails (~+5–17%), indicating higher variability and more frequent adverse extremes. the curve finance price is structurally worse, with ~+64% mean and ~+80% p99 losses, showing consistently amplified tail risk. as n increases, absolute losses decline but relative ordering is unchanged, implying that feed choice primarily affects extreme risk, not average pricing. adverse performance results for adverse performance (100k sims, top 10k), the separation across feeds becomes clearer and more directional. relative to binance, the chainlink op feed shows a small improvement (≈ −0.6% mean), with tight dispersion and limited downside (~−5%), indicating slightly more stable behavior under adverse selection. the eth feed, however, exhibits consistent deterioration: mean losses increase by ~6%, with p99 exceeding ~11% and a strongly positive median. this suggests a systematic bias toward worse execution in adverse scenarios rather than symmetric noise. the curve finance price shows the strongest degradation, with ~21% mean and ~28% p99 increases in losses, and importantly no meaningful left-tail relief (min still +13%). this indicates persistently worse outcomes under stress, consistent with liquidity-driven slippage. mean performance results for the 50k / top-50 tail simulation, differences across feeds compress substantially, indicating weaker structural divergence than in the larger-sample case. relative to binance, the chainlink op feed now shows a slight improvement in tail losses (≈ −0.9% mean), with modest dispersion and limited downside (~−7.8%). the eth feed is effectively neutral: mean slightly worse (~+0.5%) but median near zero, suggesting no systematic bias and largely symmetric deviations. the curve finance price remains the weakest, but the effect is much smaller than before: mean tail losses increase by ~4.7% and p99 by ~17%, with reduced variance and even occasional outperformance (negative min). smoothing adverse performance results under adverse performance (100k simulations, top 10k) with smoothing disabled (ema = 1), the separation across feeds becomes both clearer and more structural. to enable 1:1 comparison, our ground truth feed remains the smooth 600 ema binance feed. relative to the previously smoothed binance benchmark, all feeds exhibit a marked deterioration in adverse performance once smoothing is removed (ema = 1). this shift is broad-based: distributions move upward, tail losses increase, and previously modest differences across feeds become more pronounced. conclusion relative to the binance-based parameterisation path, chainlink feeds remain broadly comparable but with measurable deviations that depend on regime and network. in extreme tails, eth slightly improves outcomes (~−3%), while op underperforms (~+5–17%), indicating higher sensitivity to discrete updates under stress. in adverse scenarios, op becomes mildly beneficial (~−0.6%), whereas eth shows consistent deterioration (~+6% mean, ~+11% p99). in mean performance, both feeds are close to neutral (within ~±1%), with no systematic bias. regime feed mean p99 interpretation tail (500k / top 50) op +5.5% +17.4% worse in extremes eth −3.0% +6.0% slight mean improvement, worse tail adverse (100k / top 10k) op −0.6% +2.4% slight improvement eth +6.1% +11.1% consistently worse mean (50k / full) op −0.9% +6.3% near-neutral to slightly better eth +0.5% +7.9% neutral mean, worse tail removing smoothing leads to a clear deterioration across all feeds: losses increase, distributions shift upward, and previously smaller differences become more pronounced. the key takeaway is that the binance feed consistently outperforms chainlink feeds, while on average and in some adverse conditions, chainlink—particularly on op—can match or modestly outperform binance. on-chain case study: 10-10-2025 to study performance more closely, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the october 10th, 2025, market crash using ohlc data constructed from the curve oracle contract and chainlink oracle for the wbtc/crvusd pair. method data: for this, we retrieve historical price() values from the specified curve oracle of the wbtc-crvusd llammalend market over the interval 2025-10-10 00:00:00 to 2025-10-11 12:00:00 utc using an archive rpc endpoint. the extraction procedure maps the requested time window to ethereum block numbers, samples the curve oracle’s historical price() values across that block range, and adaptively refines sampling around intervals with larger price movements. each retained sample is enriched with its block timestamp and exported as json. for chainlink data, we fetch wbtc/btc, crvusd/usd, and btc/usd feed and chain them accordingly (e.g., wbtc_btc * btc_usd / crvusd_usd) to receive the wbtc/crvusd pair. chainlink vs cruve oracle price as we can see, the curve is smoother as we fetch the price from the oracle contract, meaning an ema of 600 is already applied from the oracle price. smoothing optimization: we perform two smoothing optimizations to identify ema candidates for chainlink. self-referential smoothing method: we estimate the characteristic smoothing scale of the chainlink series using an elbow (knee) detection method applied to the noise–span curve of exponential moving averages. for each candidate span, we compute a noise metric defined as the standard deviation of first differences of the ema, which decreases monotonically with increasing span. to identify the point of diminishing returns, we normalize the span and noise axes and select the point that maximizes the perpendicular distance to the straight line connecting the smallest and largest spans. referenced smoothing method: we estimate the optimal ema smoothing parameter for the chainlink feed by minimizing its tracking error relative to an external reference (curve) after strict timestamp alignment. for each candidate span ( s ), we compute ( em a s ​ ) on the chainlink price and evaluate its deviation from the curve price over the overlapping sample using metrics such as mean squared error (mse), mean absolute error (mae), and correlation. the optimal span is selected as the minimizer of mse (with correlation used as a secondary diagnostic), yielding the smoothing scale at which chainlink most closely replicates the reference process. this procedure assumes synchronous observations and implicitly treats curve as a proxy for the latent “true” price, so results are sensitive to alignment quality and any systematic lead–lag between feeds. experimental design: we conduct a deterministic sample over every possible window and conduct a sweep over changing the bands parameter (e.g., liquidity_range_values = list(range(4, 51, 4)) ). we look at the worst-case losses by calculating loss over the 50 worst windows (representing approximately, ~2.3% of the sample). experiment 1: we compare chainlink with ema = 600 against curve with ema = 1 to obtain an equivalently smoothed baseline comparison. experiment 2: we compare chainlink with optimal values to test whether comparable behavior can still be achieved under chainlink smoothing. for this, we use the self-referential smoothing method and the referenced smoothing method. for the references, we see an optimal smoothing of 16 minutes for the referenced 25 minutes. self-referential smoothing method suggesting an optimal ema time of 16 minutes (960s) referenced smoothing method suggesting an optimal ema time of 25 minutes (1500s) results the applied ema is visually displayed in the chart below. experiment 1: chainlink 600 ema vs curve 600 ema the chainlink feed seems to perform superior by 6-8% beyond band 4. at band 4, it performed 42.6% worse. experiment 2: chainlink 960 ema and 1500 ema vs curve 600 ema 16 min (960s) ema 25 min (1500s) ema cost of lag the figure below shows cross-correlations of 1-minute log returns between each feed and binance across different time lags, where the x-axis represents the lag (in minutes) and the y-axis the correlation. by construction, positive lags indicate the feed leads binance, while negative lags indicate the feed lags binance. each curve corresponds to a different price series (curve, raw chainlink, and ema-smoothed chainlink), and the location of the peak identifies the effective lead–lag relationship, while the height of the peak reflects how strongly the series co-moves with binance. thus, curves peaking further to the left indicate slower or more delayed price adjustment, whereas curves closer to zero indicate more timely alignment with the reference market. benchmarking against binance as an external reference reveals that all feeds lag the broader market, but to different degrees. curve exhibits the largest delay, with peak correlation at approximately −10 minutes, indicating it reacts significantly after binance. in contrast, chainlink is substantially more timely: the raw feed lags by only ~1 minute, and ema-smoothed variants lag by ~3–4 minutes while achieving higher correlations due to noise reduction. this indicates that chainlink is closer to real-time price discovery than curve, and that smoothing improves statistical alignment but introduces additional latency. overall, the results suggest a hierarchy of timeliness: binance → chainlink (raw) → chainlink (smoothed) → curve, with smoothing trading off responsiveness for stability. conclusion the case study suggests that, with varying degrees of smoothing, chainlink oracles can achieve better performance while remaining more responsive to market conditions. advocating for the use of chainlink oracles in production. llammasimulator: chainlink vs curve pool oracles the question in the case study unanswered is the following: “does our finding generalise to normal market conditions?”. to answer this question, we retrieve using the curve prices api oracle price feeds from the wbtc/crvusd feed of the wbtc mint market (controller address: 0x4e59541306910ad6dc1dac0ac9dfb29bd9f15c67) from 2022.03.11 to 2026.03.11. limitations sample scope: results depend on the specific time window and assets; may not generalize across regimes. binance as proxy: binance is treated as ground truth, but may not fully represent on-chain price dynamics or curve pool conditions.
