along with open questions requiring clarification. сurve-stablecoin_ai_report.pdf chainsecurity_curve_ptoracle_audit_draft.pdf findings summary id source severity title status cs-001 chainsecurity medium incorrect discount parameters check pending sm-high-01 statemind high incorrect _update_discount_params validation new sm-medium-01 statemind medium mev exploitation via immediate parameter updates new sm-info-04 statemind informational misleading "0 = no limit" comment new cs-002 chainsecurity informational code duplication new cs-003 chainsecurity informational gas savings new cs-004 chainsecurity informational incorrect comments new cs-006 chainsecurity informational missing natspec comments new cs-008 chainsecurity informational stale last_price after expiry needs research cs-009 chainsecurity informational out of date price in price_w needs research cs-note-8.1 chainsecurity note usage in llamalend markets needs research detailed findings cs-001: incorrect discount parameters check (medium) source: chainsecurity (cs-curve-pt-oracle-001) description: in _update_discount_params() , the check to ensure discount <= discount_precision uses self.slope and self.intercept (the old values) instead of the proposed _slope and _intercept values. this allows a malicious or careless manager to set new discount parameters that would cause _calculate_price() to revert due to underflow when computing discount_precision - discount , effectively making the oracle unusable. affected lines: ptoracle.vy:243-247 recommendation: validate the proposed values ( _slope , _intercept ), not the stored ones. recompute time_to_maturity_years from the current state and compute new_discount using _slope and _intercept , then assert new_discount < discount_precision before updating storage. sm-high-01: incorrect _update_discount_params validation (high) source: statemind ai description: same issue as cs-001. _update_discount_params validates using the current self.slope / self.intercept instead of the proposed _slope / _intercept , so unsafe new values can be accepted, and later cause reverts when used at runtime. impact: protocol-wide dos: if discount > discount_precision , discount_factor underflows and reverts under checked arithmetic, breaking price() and price_w() across the system. affected lines: ptoracle.vy:243-247 recommendation: enforce the invariant 0 <= discount < discount_precision end-to-end and document it validate the proposed values, not the stored ones recompute time_to_maturity_years from the current state and compute new_discount using _slope and _intercept assert new_discount < discount_precision before updating storage include clear revert messages optionally cap acceptable discounts further (e.g., <= 95% of discount_precision ) to reduce risk from extreme settings sm-medium-01: mev exploitation via immediate parameter updates (medium) source: statemind ai description: ptoracle's pricing parameters are updated via set_linear_discount set_slope_from_apy and take effect immediately. the update gating uses a strict inequality check block.timestamp > last_discount_update + min_update_interval . because min_update_interval can be configured to 0, and there is no timelock or commit-reveal. updates can be executed as frequently as once per block/second and applied atomically. mev exposure: bots can monitor the mempool for parameter-update transactions, front-run trades at the old price, let the update execute, and then back-run at the new price to capture the discrete price jump. impact: mev/sandwich risk: attackers can front-run on old parameters and back-run on new parameters to arbitrage the discrete price change volatility and coordination risk: managers can rapidly flip parameters (especially with min_update_interval = 0 ) reputational and financial impact from predictable, profitable mev opportunities affected lines: ptoracle.vy:262-270, 274-305, 318-320 recommendation: add delay/commit mechanisms: implement a two-step commit-reveal scheme or a timelock enforce sensible lower bounds and cooldowns: set a non-zero minimum for min_update_interval , add per-parameter cooldowns, cap maximum change per interval correct the rate-limit predicate: change to >= so effective interval matches configured value, or document the current strict behavior and rename variable (e.g., min_seconds_before_next_update ) reduce discrete jumps: introduce gradual/ramped transitions so parameter changes phase in over time execution privacy: use private transaction channels (e.g., flashbots) when executing updates sm-info-04: misleading "0 = no limit" comment (informational) source: statemind ai description: the comment on max_slope_change and max_intercept_change says "0 = no limit", but the implementation uses change <= limit and the constructor initializes both limits to max_value(uint256) as the real "no limit" sentinel. with this logic, a limit of 0 actually forbids any non-zero change (hard freeze), while max_value(uint256) behaves as unbounded. impact: admins following the comment may set a limit to 0, expecting "no limit", but instead freeze discount updates until limits are raised again. this is a misconfiguration/ux risk causing temporary dos of parameter updates. affected lines: ptoracle.vy:45-49, 124-129, 219-235 recommendation: update comments to match behavior (e.g., max_uint = no limit; 0 = no change allowed ) and/or adjust the code so that 0 truly means "no limit" by skipping the check when the limit is 0. add tests and docs that explicitly cover 0, bounded values, and max_value(uint256) semantics. informational findings (code quality) cs-002: code duplication (informational) source: chainsecurity (cs-curve-pt-oracle-002) description: _update_discount_params() and _calculate_price() both contain the same logic to compute the discount, which is currently duplicated. this logic could be refactored into a separate internal function to reduce code duplication and improve maintainability. cs-003: gas savings (informational) source: chainsecurity (cs-curve-pt-oracle-003) description: the following gas optimizations were identified: pt could be made immutable, as it is set only once in the constructor underlying_oracle could be made immutable, as it is set only once in the constructor in __init__() , when logging priceupdated , the storage load of self.last_price could be avoided as the value was stored just before in _update_discount_params , self.slope and self.intercept are loaded from storage multiple times. caching them in local variables would save gas. cs-004: incorrect comments (informational) source: chainsecurity (cs-curve-pt-oracle-004) description: the comment "0 = no limit" for max_slope_change and max_intercept_change is incorrect - 0 actually prevents any change (covered by sm-info-04) the comment "rate limiting for set_linear_discount" on last_discount_update is misleading as this variable is also used in set_slope_from_apy() cs-006: missing natspec comments (informational) source: chainsecurity (cs-curve-pt-oracle-006) description: except for set_slope_from_apy() all external functions lack natspec comments describing their purpose, parameters, and return values. while the function names are mostly self-explanatory, adding natspec comments would enhance code readability and maintainability. items requiring research & response cs-009: out-of-date price in price_w function source: chainsecurity (cs-curve-pt-oracle-009) priority: medium description: while price() always returns up-to-date prices with respect to the underlying price oracle, price_w() might return a cached price if: expiry has not been reached yet the last call to price_w() was in the same block as the current call in such a case, the function returns self.last_price . this could be problematic if the underlying price oracle can have multiple updates in the same block, as the pt oracle would not reflect the latest of those updates. research questions: what underlying oracles will be used? (chainlink, custom, etc.) can those oracles update multiple times within a single block? how does llamalend call price_w() ? could same-block staleness cause issues? are the gas savings from caching worth the potential staleness? possible outcomes: accept: document the behavior clearly for integrators fix: remove same-block caching or add parameter version tracking cs-008: stale last_price after expiry source: chainsecurity (cs-curve-pt-oracle-008) priority: medium description: after the pt expiry, the price returned by price_w() is no longer stored in last_price . integrators relying on the stored price may be affected if they do not switch to calling the view function price() instead. research questions: are there any integrators (including llamalend) that read last_price directly instead of calling price() or price_w() ? should last_price should the price be updated to the underlying price after expiry for consistency? is there a reason not to update last_price after expiry (gas savings)? possible outcomes: accept: document that last_price is not updated post-expiry fix: update last_price in price_w() even after expiry cs-note-8.1: usage of oracle in curve llamalend markets source: chainsecurity (note 8.1) priority: high description: this oracle is intended to be used as a collateral price oracle for curve llamalend markets. by design, the price of this oracle does not reflect the actual market price of the pt token, but rather an estimate based on a linear function. this design choice carries non-trivial economic implications when used in a curve llamalend amm, as it can lead to situations where the oracle price diverges significantly from the market price, potentially causing unexpected liquidations or missed trading opportunities. research questions: what is the maximum acceptable divergence between the oracle price and the pt market price? how will borrowers be protected from liquidation when the market price drops but the oracle price remains higher? conversely, how will the protocol be protected when the oracle price is lower than the market price (undercollateralization risk)? should there be circuit breakers or monitoring for extreme divergence? what documentation is needed for llamalend users to understand this risk? deliverables: risk analysis document outlining divergence scenarios recommended parameter ranges for slope/intercept to minimize divergence user-facing documentation explaining the pricing model and risks open questions (chainsecurity) design decision: set_linear_discount vs set_slope_from_apy both functions set discount parameters, but have different behaviors: why are both needed? the intercept and slope can be easily calculated off-chain from the apy, or vice versa. why does one function allow setting the intercept and the other always set it to 0? what are the practical scenarios where the intercept must be set to non-zero values? project management tasks to manage these tasks effectively, for those requiring code changes, create a branch in the ptoracle repository named with the appropriate reference. after completing the changes, submit a pull request to the audit branch. excerpt: Audit Report : PT Oracle Code Assessment Audit Date : 25 November 2025 Fix PR : https://github.com/llama-risk/curve-ptoracle-vy/pull/9 Findings Summary ID Severity Title Status CS-CURVE-PT-ORACLE-001 Medium Incorrect Discount Para
searchText: chainsecurity audit response research pt-oracle's oracle design audit report : pt oracle code assessment audit date : 25 november 2025 fix pr : https://github.com/llama-risk/curve-ptoracle-vy/pull/9 findings summary id severity title status cs-curve-pt-oracle-001 medium incorrect discount parameters check fixed cs-curve-pt-oracle-002 informational code duplication fixed cs-curve-pt-oracle-003 informational gas savings fixed cs-curve-pt-oracle-004 informational incorrect comments fixed cs-curve-pt-oracle-005 informational indexed event fixed cs-curve-pt-oracle-006 informational missing natspec comments fixed cs-curve-pt-oracle-007 informational price bump acknowledged cs-curve-pt-oracle-008 informational stale last_price after expiry acknowledged cs-curve-pt-oracle-009 informational out of date price in price_w function acknowledged acknowledged findings cs-curve-pt-oracle-007: price bump price jumps at expiry (if intercept != 0) and on parameter updates are inherent to the linear discount model. mitigated by: max_slope_change and max_intercept_change limits constrain update magnitudes managers are expected to reduce intercept gradually as expiry approaches [operational: document parameter management best practices] cs-curve-pt-oracle-008: stale last_price after expiry intentional behavior. post-expiry, both price() and price_w() return the underlying oracle price directly. the last_price storage is not updated to save gas since caching provides no benefit after expiry. cs-curve-pt-oracle-009: out of date price in price_w function same-block caching is a deliberate gas optimization. underlying oracle considerations : chainlink: cannot have multiple updates per block - no staleness concern custom oracle: may have multiple updates, but practical impact is minimal within a single block if fresh price is required : use the price() view function which always computes current price. open questions 6.1 design decision: set_linear_discount vs set_slope_from_apy why are both needed? function purpose set_slope_from_apy() standard operation - specify target apy, contract calculates slope set_linear_discount() direct parameter control for edge cases set_slope_from_apy() is simpler for routine use ("i want x% apy"). set_linear_discount() provides full control when needed. why does one function allow setting the intercept and the other always sets it to 0? the apy formula assumes pure time-decay (intercept = 0). this ensures: no price discontinuity at expiry clean apy-to-slope relationship what are the practical scenarios where the intercept must be set to non-zero values? the intercept effectively shifts the oracle price along the y-axis. since lowering the intercept would directly reduce prices and could prematurely trigger liquidations, we do not anticipate adjusting the intercept downward. however, there are practical scenarios where increasing the intercept may be necessary. this can be required when the observed market price deviates materially from the oracle price, for example due to: supply–demand imbalances in the pendle amm , which can cause persistent deviations from fair value. fundamental changes in the underlying apy , driven by structural or economic factors rather than short-term volatility. if there is a structural shift in the underlying earnings and the discount model is systematically underpricing the pt, we may choose to adjust both the intercept and the slope so that the oracle better reflects the true underlying value. adjusting only the slope can lead to undesirable behavior, such as the discounted price reaching parity with the underlying asset too early or too late relative to maturity. for instance, if the slope is increased too aggressively, parity may be reached well before the intended maturity window. in such cases, jointly adjusting both the slope and the intercept allows parity to be reached at the appropriate time while preserving a more reasonable and gradual discount price path. additionally, during market initialization and near maturity, pt markets tend to exhibit low liquidity and elevated volatility. in these periods, markets may be paused and only activated once sufficient liquidity and stability are present. upon activation, the oracle price must accurately reflect the underlying asset, and having the flexibility to set a non-zero intercept allows the model to align with observed market conditions from the outset. notes 8.1 usage of the oracle in curve llamalend markets acknowledged. the deterministic linear model may diverge from market prices. the core reason we use a linear discount model is that pt markets are mainly used by loopers with very high ltvs. this makes these positions sensitive to small price fluctuations. the market price is too volatile and would result in a lot of unnecessary liquidations. we can leverage the fixed-yield property of pt markets to build an oracle with a much more stable price and offer a safer experience for loopers. also to scale llamalend markets safely we would like to move away from being dependent on single-pool oracles in general. we expect divergence with market price especially in long-dated pt markets. this is the reason we introduce the ability to update parameters. the model will be updated if a significant deviation is detected. the bounds for parameter updates need to be determined separately for each asset. the model will be less risky in the sense that there will be less liquidations for the user compared to using a market oracle. we also introduce safety bounds so that an incorrect parameter update wouldn’t result in a big catastrophe. 8.2 admin_role cannot be granted or revoked intentional design. the admin can renounce but not transfer the role. for admin rotation, deploy a new oracle. admin rotation is a last resort risk mitigation action that dao can leverage to intervene in case the current admin is performing poorly or maliciously

excerpt: How the oracle choice affects Lllamalend Scenario 1: Simple Arbitrage We agree that Scenario 1 is a real and important edge case, and it correctly illustrates how a predictable oracle path combined with market–oracle divergence ca
searchText: comments on chainsecurity responses for pendle pts research pt-oracle's oracle design how the oracle choice affects lllamalend scenario 1: simple arbitrage we agree that scenario 1 is a real and important edge case, and it correctly illustrates how a predictable oracle path combined with market–oracle divergence can create adverse flows. that said, we believe it is equally important to consider the direction of mispricing, as overpricing pt collateral introduces asymmetric and, in practice, more severe risks than underpricing. when pt collateral is overpriced relative to the market, llamalend is exposed to structurally worse outcomes: borrowers can extract excess credit against inflated collateral, liquidations are delayed or softened, and the protocol risks ending up long collateral at prices that cannot be realized externally. in the extreme, this leads to bad debt and socialized losses. by contrast, underpricing primarily manifests as conservative behavior: higher collateral requirements, earlier liquidations, and reduced borrowing capacity. these outcomes are visible and potentially uncomfortable, but they are loss-limiting for the system, not loss-amplifying. from a risk-management perspective, this asymmetry is the core reason we prefer configurations that err on the side of underpricing rather than overpricing. more generally, it is important to emphasize that this class of issue is not unique to the proposed oracle. any oracle that does not directly use the instantaneous market price will, at times, diverge from it. even market-based oracles introduce similar dynamics via filtering windows, smoothing, lags, and anti-manipulation measures, all of which can create temporary arbitrage opportunities. using the raw market price directly does not eliminate this problem; it merely shifts it into a different form, often with worse tail risks. in that sense, the behavior observed here is expected rather than exceptional. the design choice, therefore, is not about eliminating arbitrage entirely, but about choosing which failure modes are acceptable. given the asymmetric risks discussed above, we deliberately prefer controlled underpricing with bounded convergence over configurations that risk persistent overpricing. with careful calibration of the slope, buffers, and update cadence, and with timely parameter adjustments when deviations grow too large, the impact of these edge cases can be minimized without exposing the system to the more dangerous downside of overvalued collateral. scenario 2: buy and hold the concern correctly identifies that the proposed mechanism introduces a deterministic, linear convergence of the oracle price toward maturity, rather than relying on a fully free-floating market price. in that sense, the price path is exogenous, and the critique is directionally valid at a purely mechanical level. however, this is not fundamentally different from how pendle pts or fixed-income bonds behave, where prices predictably converge toward face value as maturity approaches. in both cases, the convergence path is known in advance and creates a carry-type opportunity rather than an informational arbitrage. in theory, the profit an arbitrageur can extract from this mechanism is upper-bounded by the carry obtained from simply buying and holding the pt until maturity, and in practice is often lower on an annualised basis once liquidity constraints, slippage, funding costs, and arbitrage dynamics are taken into account. the mechanism therefore introduces a controlled convergence path whose economic impact is constrained by liquidity and arbitrage, rather than creating an exploitable pricing asymmetry. oracle jumps although we won’t have the ability to directly update the oracle price itself with the current oracle contract, we have the option to update parameters of the linear model in which case the intercept term adjustments can cause price jumps. we agree with the underlying heuristic: when correcting toward market prices, gradual or rate-limited adjustments are preferable to large instantaneous moves, even if the final price is more accurate. it is generally undesirable to have a big deviation between market price and the oracle price due to competitiveness. however the adjustments should also be carefully considered as not to create an opportunity for extraction. we will take this consideration further into account when calibrating offset updates and evaluating parameter adjustment cadence, with the goal of minimizing unnecessary extraction while preserving the conservative bias against collateral overpricing. reference chainsecurity: response to llamarisk on discount-based oracle for pendle pts .pdf

searchText: transition memo  prepared for the incoming risk team, assuming responsibility for curve protocol risk management, previously held by llamarisk (llama consulting ltd.). 1. where are we now? scope of work llamarisk provides research, parameter analysis, monitoring, and advisory services to the curve dao. the engagement primarily focuses on the llamma and crvusd product lines: crvusd — stablecoin mint markets, pegkeeper pools, and peg stability llamalend (v1 and v2) — isolated lending markets using llamma soft-liquidation yieldbasis — while not a direct engagement focus, interdependency with crvusd necessitates attention here the work is shared with swiss stake , who handles software development, bd, deployment coordination, and technical/community support. llamarisk's role is analytical and advisory: asset risk reviews, preparation of governance recommendations for the dao's consideration, market parameterisation analysis, exposure calibration, monitoring, and advisory support during incidents. for the avoidance of doubt, llamarisk does not deploy markets, hold deployment authority, custody assets, or execute governance actions; those functions rest with the curve dao and its operational partners. product state llamalend v2 is in early rollout. three pilot markets (wsteth/eth, wsteth/usdc, wbtc/usdc) launched on optimism on june 11, 2026, supported by a 100k op incentive grant, second half has been granted. mainnet market candidates are syrupusdc, susdf , sfrxusd and sdola. susdf shows a high-risk profile and little support for falcon finance; we leave the analysis for reference and advise against onboarding. the v2 rollout is the most active workstream at handover. llamalend v1 remains live on ethereum mainnet. deprecation has been largely facilitated by llamarisk, but additional coordination is required with stakedao, convex, and resupply, all of whom have integrations built on v1 markets. no unilateral deprecation should occur. most v1 markets without significant tvl have been deprecated. crvusd operates with active mint markets and pegkeeper pools. peg stability continues to require active monitoring, implementation of stabilization strategies, and parameter management. there is significant exposure to yieldbasis, which is largely responsible for stabilization challenges. yieldbasis exposure is capped using a pegkeeper absorption capacity model. a recent yieldbasis upgrade may change the relationship between yb exposure and crvusd sell pressure. impaired markets the sdola/crvusd llamalend market was exploited on march 2, 2026 via a flash-loan attack combining a permissionless llamma exchange with oracle manipulation through dolasavings.stake() . refer to the report for more details. 27 of 30 borrowers were hard-liquidated (~$10.9m debt), with ~$766k in borrower losses. a full post-mortem is documented. a repayment proposal has been tabled to the dao. llamarisk's position paper clarifies that llamarisk (llama consulting ltd.) did not deploy the market and does not hold deployment authority, and that the repayment proposal is a governance contribution provided for the dao's consideration that does not constitute, and shall not be construed as, an admission of fault, responsibility, or liability by llamarisk. the crv/crvusd recovery mechanism introduces a market-based path for addressing bad debt, but its effectiveness should not be assumed. further analysis is required to assess whether the mechanism materially improves recovery outcomes, whether it can scale beyond the crv/crvusd market, and whether it offers a credible alternative to direct dao repayment. emergency dao (edao) the edao's current powers cover crvusd debt ceiling reduction, monetary policy changes, amm fee adjustments, pool pause/unpause, gauge killing, erc20 recovery, and psr pause. some critical powers are not yet active . a detailed spec for proposed edao additions is included in the package (see edao safety actions — spec ), covering borrow cap reduction, oracle swapping, aggregated pricing removal, and monetary policy levers. additionally, swiss stake had previously begun development of a delegation proxy contract, allowing the dao to designate a whitelisted operator that has authority over specific parameters with bounds on magnitude and time delay on execution. our advice is to continue the development of this delegation system and set the independent risk team as the whitelisted operator. 2. what is the current operating baseline? frameworks and processes three risk frameworks are in place and should be used as-is (with attribution per the licensing terms documented in the frameworks section): collateral onboarding framework — four-layer asset assessment (fundamentals, market risk, technological risk, counterparty risk) followed by llamma-specific parameterisation (oracle, a, fee, discounts, exposure, monetary policy). version 1.0, dated april 6, 2026. pegkeeper framework — five-section assessment covering stablecoin fundamentals, performance analytics, on-chain management, regulation/compliance, and pegkeeper suitability. outputs a dao-facing recommendation with debt ceiling guidance. bd asset pre-screening — lightweight pass/fail gate before full review. hard criteria include ≤2% slippage on $2.5m swap, viable oracle path, and economic viability for lending collateral; ≥$2–3m pool liquidity, 1-year trading history, and no material depegs for pegkeeper candidates. the asset onboarding process routes through: bd pre-screen (swiss stake, ~3 days) → in-depth review (llamarisk, 5–10 days) → dao vote (joint, ~7 days) → deployment. assets that fail pre-screening are blocked from reapplying for 3 months. quantitative methods four methods are documented and operational: llamma market parameters (a, fee, loan discount, liquidation discount) — calibrated using the llammasimulator v2 . parameters are assessed jointly, not independently. oracle smoothing choice must be determined before running the simulator. exposure / borrow cap / debt ceiling — stress-tested against a 99% expected shortfall price shock, adjusted for llamma soft-liquidation efficiency, stressed dex executable liquidity (using the deepest single route, not summed), and a liquidity contraction factor. a fresh-market variant exists for pre-launch cap estimation. irm optimization — simulation-based interest rate model tuning combining empirical utilization-target estimation, regime-window selection, reduced-form utilization dynamics, monte carlo simulation, and multi-objective optimization. a note in the document advises considering simpler methods anchored to current market rates for agility. yb safe caps — estimates maximum yieldbasis exposure from pegkeeper pool absorption capacity, incorporating real-time pool imbalance state via ema-smoothed crvusd inventory share. a liquidity shock modelling methodology is also documented, constructing empirical slippage curves from dex aggregator quotes and decomposing shocks into level (depth contraction) and shape (structural distortion) components. key finding: liquidity shocks are predominantly depth contractions (~1.4–1.6x at p90) rather than structural curve reshaping. llamalend v2 decisions already made optimism markets : params finalized, oracles verified, incentives structured (see timeline doc). oracle approach for op : single chainlink /usd feeds through a chainlinkema wrapper (20 observations, 30s interval). mainnet candidates : syrupusdc, sdola, sfrxusd, and susdf (recommend against) identified . 3. what could go wrong? immediate operational risks risk context sdola repayment governance unresolved governance process. the donation gauge concept, bad debt recovery mechanism, and repayment funding source all need resolution. political sensitivity — handle carefully. edao powers not fully activated vault deposit caps depend on v2 blueprint deployment. until these are live, emergency response options are limited. v1 deprecation coordination stakedao, convex, and resupply have products built on llv1. premature deprecation will break integrations and create political fallout. sfrxusd market redeployment the sfrxusd llamalend market has an immutable oracle for which the referenced pool is low liquidity. redeployment using the pegkeeper pool oracle is pending. resupply are waiting for this. crvusd stability yieldbasis exposure has necessitated heightened attention to stabilization strategies, including parameter optimization, incentive management, and the integration of novel stabilization designs. this continues to be a precarious dependency on crvusd stability, which needs special attention. systemic risks to monitor oracle manipulation — no general methodology exists yet for assessing oracle manipulation risk across curve lending, mint, and pool oracle designs. this is a documented future research topic flagged as high priority. vault pps manipulation — the sdola attack exploited an unsmoothed converttoassets() read. other vault collaterals (sfrax, sfrxusd, susds, yearn v3) use different accounting and are not currently vulnerable, but any future vault-based collateral must be assessed for atomic manipulation of totalassets() . methodology gaps pegkeeper debt ceiling methodology — no quantitative method exists for setting pegkeeper debt ceilings. currently set by judgment. oracle manipulation methodology — no systematic framework for assessing manipulation cost, required capital, or monitoring indicators. yb safe cap v2 — the current heuristic is linear and does not model nonlinear price impact or yb-side source capacity. coupled llamma–pool simulation — the simulator treats price paths as exogenous and cannot capture the feedback loop between llamma selling and external market prices. 4. what should the next owner do first? week 1: orientation and continuity read the edao safety actions spec in full. understand what emergency powers exist, what is missing, and what the activation path looks like. coordinate with swiss stake on implementation priority. support roll out of llamalend v2. understand what emergency powers exist, what is missing, and what the activation path looks like. coordinate with swiss stake and resupply (resupply is a crucial partner for bootstrapping markets) on implementation priority. run the collateral onboarding framework, then parameterise using the llammasimulator. weeks 2–4: operational takeover take over the llamalend v2 monitoring. the markets launched june. monitor utilization, borrower behavior, oracle health, and incentive effectiveness. the 100k op grant runs for 4 weekly epochs — the last epoch is in early july. coordinate the mainnet llv2 markets deployment. this includes configuration and deployment of initial mainnet markets, governance execution on curve (gauge votes), and governance proceedings on resupply (supporting analysis and recommendations to resupply forum). review and advance the swiss stake bd pipeline. handoff items include additional pegkeeper pools, additional mint markets, dao reserve strategy, unibtc/wstlink v2 interest, and broader llamalend v2 ecosystem integrations (resupply readiness, pt market bootstrapping). the risk team should not perform bd responsibility- coordinate with the swiss stake bd team and support them in the risk function to achieve their business objectives. beyond: strategic items develop the oracle manipulation methodology. this is the most important missing analytical capability. without it, future market onboarding lacks a systematic framework for assessing manipulation risk. oracle solution: only assets with deep curve pools are being used as an oracle source in llamalend, which severely limits scalability. a more manipulation-resistant and durable solution (i.e., tolerance for liquidity venue shifting) is crucial to scale llamalend. develop the pegkeeper debt ceiling methodology. currently set by judgment, a quantitative or semi-quantitative approach is needed. develop a method to manage crvusd stability and yb exposure: once post-upgrade yieldbasis pool data is available, update m y b ​ based on observed sell-pressure dynamics. plan v1 deprecation in full. begin stakeholder coordination with stakedao, convex, and resupply. deprecation should be gradual, joint, and announced well in advance. key contacts and coordination points party role coordination surface swiss stake bd,
